The 1968 title song featuring the opening lines of the album: "If I ventured in the slipstream between the viaducts of your dream". His early voice was described as "flinty and tender, beseeching and plaintive".[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-O'Hagan,_Sean-91)

* * *

_Problems playing this file? See [media help](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Media "Help:Media")._

Morrison's first album for Warner Bros Records was _Astral Weeks_ (which he had already performed in several clubs around Boston), a mystical [song cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Song_cycle "Song cycle"), often considered to be his best work and one of the best albums of all time.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-AS2008-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusicAW-93)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage223-94) Morrison has said, "When _Astral Weeks_ came out, I was starving, _literally_."[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage100-95) Released in 1968, the album originally received an indifferent response from the public, but it eventually achieved critical acclaim.

The album is described by [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic")'s William Ruhlmann as hypnotic, meditative, and as possessing a unique musical power.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusicAW-93) It has been compared to French [Impressionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impressionism "Impressionism") and mystical Celtic poetry.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-96)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-97)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage88,99-98) A 2004 _Rolling Stone_ magazine review begins with the words: "This is music of such enigmatic beauty that thirty-five years after its release, _Astral Weeks_ still defies easy, admiring description."[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RS19-99)[Alan Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Light_(journalist) "Alan Light (journalist)") later described _Astral Weeks_ as "like nothing he had done previously—and really, nothing anyone had done previously. Morrison sings of lost love, death, and nostalgia for childhood in the Celtic soul that would become his signature."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Astral_Weeks,_Light-12) It has been placed on many lists of best albums of all time. In the 1995 _Mojo_ list of 100 Best Albums, it was listed as number two and was number nineteen on the _Rolling Stone_ magazine's "[500 Greatest Albums of All Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone's_500_Greatest_Albums_of_All_Time "Rolling Stone's 500 Greatest Albums of All Time")" in 2003.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-100)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-500_Greatest_Albums-101) In December 2009, it was voted the top Irish album of all time by a poll of leading Irish musicians conducted by _[Hot Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot\_Press "Hot Press")_ magazine.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-102)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-103)

### _Moondance_ to _Into the Music_: 1970–1979

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Moondance to Into the Music: 1970–1979")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Van_Morrison_%281972%29.png/250px-Van_Morrison_%281972%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Van_Morrison_(1972).png)

Morrison in 1972

Morrison's third solo album, _[Moondance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moondance "Moondance")_, which was released in 1970, became his first million selling album and reached number twenty-nine on the Billboard charts.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage95-104)[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage98-105)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-106) The style of _Moondance_ stood in contrast to that of _[Astral Weeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astral\_Weeks "Astral Weeks")_. Whereas _Astral Weeks_ had a sorrowful and vulnerable tone, _Moondance_ restored a more optimistic and cheerful message to his music,[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-YorkePage69-107) which abandoned the previous record's abstract folk compositions in favour of more formally composed songs and a lively [rhythm and blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhythm_and_blues "Rhythm and blues") style he expanded on throughout his career.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-108)

The title track, although not released in the US as a single until 1977, received heavy play in [FM radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FM_broadcasting "FM broadcasting") formats.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage250-109) "[Into the Mystic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Into_the_Mystic "Into the Mystic")" has also gained a wide following over the years.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusic_Biography:_Van_Morrison-110)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-111) "[Come Running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come_Running "Come Running")", which reached the [American Top 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Top_40 "American Top 40"), rescued Morrison from what seemed then as Hot 100 obscurity.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusic.com-112)_Moondance_ was both well received and favourably reviewed. [Lester Bangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bangs "Lester Bangs") and [Greil Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greil_Marcus "Greil Marcus") had a combined full-page review in _Rolling Stone_, saying Morrison now had "the striking imagination of a consciousness that is visionary in the strongest sense of the word."[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Marcus,_Bangs-113) "That was the type of band I dig," Morrison said of the _Moondance_ sessions. "Two horns and a rhythm section—they're the type of bands that I like best." He produced the album himself as he felt like nobody else knew what he wanted.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage226-114)_Moondance_ was listed at number sixty-five on the _Rolling Stone_ magazine's _The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time_.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-500_Greatest_Albums-101) In March 2007, _Moondance_ was listed as number seventy-two on the [NARM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Recording_Merchandisers "National Association of Recording Merchandisers")[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") list of the "Definitive 200".[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Narm-115)

Over the next few years, he released a succession of albums, starting with a second one in 1970. _[His Band and the Street Choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/His\_Band\_and\_the\_Street\_Choir "His Band and the Street Choir")_ had a freer, more relaxed sound than _Moondance_, but not the _perfection_, in the opinion of critic [Jon Landau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Landau "Jon Landau"), who felt like "a few more numbers with a gravity of 'Street Choir' would have made this album as perfect as anyone could have stood."[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HBATSC-116) It contained the hit single "[Domino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domino_(Van_Morrison_song) "Domino (Van Morrison song)")", which charted at number nine in the [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-CollisPage122-117)

In 1971, he released another well-received album, _[Tupelo Honey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tupelo\_Honey "Tupelo Honey")_.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage259-118) This album produced the hit single "[Wild Night](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wild_Night "Wild Night")" that was later covered by [John Mellencamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mellencamp "John Mellencamp") and [Meshell Ndegeocello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meshell_Ndegeocello "Meshell Ndegeocello"). The title song has a notably country-soul feel about it[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-119) and the album ended with another country tune, "[Moonshine Whiskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moonshine_Whiskey "Moonshine Whiskey")". Morrison said he originally intended to make an all-country album.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage267-268-120) The recordings were as live as possible—after rehearsing the songs the musicians would enter the studio and play a whole set in one take.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-121) His co-producer, [Ted Templeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Templeman "Ted Templeman"), described this recording process as the "scariest thing I've ever seen. When he's got something together, he wants to put it down right away with no overdubbing."[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage137-122)

Released in 1972, _[Saint Dominic's Preview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint\_Dominic's\_Preview "Saint Dominic's Preview")_ revealed Morrison's break from the more accessible style of his previous three albums and moving back towards the more daring, adventurous, and meditative aspects of _Astral Weeks_. The combination of two styles of music demonstrated a versatility not previously found in his earlier albums.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Saint_Dominic's_Preview_Music_Review-123) Two songs, "[Jackie Wilson Said (I'm in Heaven When You Smile)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Wilson_Said_(I'm_in_Heaven_When_You_Smile) "Jackie Wilson Said (I'm in Heaven When You Smile)")" and "[Redwood Tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redwood_Tree_(song) "Redwood Tree (song)")", reached the Hot 100 singles chart.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusic.com-112) The songs "[Listen to the Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Listen_to_the_Lion "Listen to the Lion")" and "[Almost Independence Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_Independence_Day "Almost Independence Day")" are each over ten minutes long and employ the type of poetic imagery not heard since _Astral Weeks_.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Saint_Dominic's_Preview_Music_Review-123)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage255-256-124) It was his highest-charting album in the US until his Top Ten debut on [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") in 2008.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Charts_&_Awards-125)

He released his next album, _[Hard Nose the Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard\_Nose\_the\_Highway "Hard Nose the Highway")_, in 1973, receiving mixed, but mostly negative, reviews. The album contained the popular song "[Warm Love](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warm_Love "Warm Love")" but otherwise has been largely dismissed critically.[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage265-267-126) In a 1973 _Rolling Stone_ review, it was described as: "psychologically complex, musically somewhat uneven and lyrically excellent."[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HNTH-127)

During a three-week vacation visit to Ireland in October 1973, Morrison wrote seven of the songs that made up his next album, _[Veedon Fleece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veedon\_Fleece "Veedon Fleece")_.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage122-128) Though it attracted scant initial attention, its critical stature grew markedly over the years—with _Veedon Fleece_ now often considered to be one of Morrison's most impressive and poetic works.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage301-129)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-130) In a 2008 _Rolling Stone_ review, Andy Greene writes that when released in late 1974: "it was greeted by a collective shrug by the rock critical establishment" and concludes: "He's released many wonderful albums since, but he's never again hit the majestic heights of this one."[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Veedon_Fleece-131) "[You Don't Pull No Punches, but You Don't Push the River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You_Don't_Pull_No_Punches,_but_You_Don't_Push_the_River "You Don't Pull No Punches, but You Don't Push the River")", one of the album's side closers, exemplifies the long, hypnotic, cryptic Morrison with its references to visionary poet [William Blake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Blake "William Blake") and to the seemingly [Grail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Grail "Holy Grail")-like Veedon Fleece object.[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage300-132)

Morrison took three years to release a follow-up album. After a decade without taking time off, he said in an interview, he needed to get away from music completely and ceased listening to it for several months.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage306-133) Also suffering from [writer's block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writer's_block "Writer's block"), he seriously considered leaving the music business for good.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage305-134) Speculation that an extended [jam session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jam_session "Jam session") would be released either under the title _Mechanical Bliss_, or _Naked in the Jungle_, or _Stiff Upper Lip_, came to nothing,[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPages304-306-135) and Morrison's next album was _[A Period of Transition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Period\_of\_Transition "A Period of Transition")_ in 1977, a collaboration with [Dr. John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._John "Dr. John"), who had appeared at _[The Last Waltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_Waltz "The Last Waltz")_ concert with Morrison in 1976. The album received a mild critical reception and marked the beginning of a very prolific period of song-making.

> _[Into the Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Into\_the\_Music "Into the Music")_: The album's last four songs, "Angelou", "And the Healing Has Begun", and "It's All in the Game/You Know What They're Writing About" are a veritable tour-de-force with Morrison summoning every vocal trick at his disposal from Angelou's climactic shouts to the sexually-charged, half-mumbled monologue in "And the Healing Has Begun" to the barely audible whisper that is the album's final sound.

The following year, Morrison released _[Wavelength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength\_(album) "Wavelength (album)")_; it became at that time the fastest-selling album of his career and soon went gold.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage210-136) The title track became a modest hit, peaking at number forty-two. Making use of 1970s synthesisers, it mimics the sounds of the [shortwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shortwave "Shortwave") radio stations he listened to in his youth.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Wavelength_song_review-137) The opening track, "Kingdom Hall"—the name given by [Jehovah's Witnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jehovah's_Witnesses "Jehovah's Witnesses") to their [places of worship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_Hall "Kingdom Hall")—evoked Morrison's childhood experiences of religion with his mother,[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage210-136) and foretold the religious themes that were more evident on his next album, _[Into the Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Into\_the\_Music "Into the Music")_.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Timepieces_ITM-138)

Considered by [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") as "the definitive post-classic-era Morrison",[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-139)_Into the Music_ was released in the last year of the 1970s. Songs on this album for the first time alluded to the healing power of music, which became an abiding interest of Morrison's.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HagePage89-140) "[Bright Side of the Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bright_Side_of_the_Road "Bright Side of the Road")" was a joyful, uplifting song that is featured on the soundtrack of the movie, _[Michael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael\_(1996\_film) "Michael (1996 film)")_.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Van_Morrison_at_IMDb-141)

### _Common One_ to _Avalon Sunset_: 1980–1989

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Common One to Avalon Sunset: 1980–1989")]

With his next album, the new decade found Morrison following his [muse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muse "Muse") into uncharted territory and sometimes merciless reviews.[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage364-142)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage330-143) In February 1980, Morrison and a group of musicians travelled to Super Bear, a studio in the [French Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Alps "French Alps"), to record (on the site of a former [abbey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abbey "Abbey")) what is considered to be the most controversial album in his discography; later "Morrison admitted his original concept was even more esoteric than the final product."[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage230-144)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage365-145) The album, _[Common One](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common\_One "Common One")_, consisted of six songs; the longest, "[Summertime in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summertime_in_England "Summertime in England")", lasted fifteen and a half minutes and ended with the words _"Can you feel the silence?"_. _[NME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NME "NME")_ magazine's [Paul Du Noyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Du_Noyer "Paul Du Noyer") called the album "colossally smug and cosmically dull; an interminable, vacuous and drearily egotistical stab at spirituality: Into the muzak."[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage230-144)[Greil Marcus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greil_Marcus "Greil Marcus"), whose previous writings had been favourably inclined towards Morrison, critically remarked: "It's Van acting the part of the 'mystic poet' he thinks he's supposed to be."[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage364-142) Morrison insisted the album was never "meant to be a commercial album."[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage364-142) Biographer [Clinton Heylin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinton_Heylin "Clinton Heylin") concludes: "He would not attempt anything so ambitious again. Henceforth every radical idea would be tempered by some notion of commerciality."[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage365-145) Later, critics reassessed the album more favourably with the success of "Summertime in England".[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage365-145)[Lester Bangs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lester_Bangs "Lester Bangs") wrote in 1982, "Van was making holy music even though he thought he was, and us rock critics had made our usual mistake of paying too much attention to the lyrics."[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage364-142)

Morrison's next album, _[Beautiful Vision](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beautiful\_Vision "Beautiful Vision")_, released in 1982, had him returning once again to the music of his Northern Irish roots.[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage338-146) Well received by the critics and public, it produced a minor UK hit single, "[Cleaning Windows](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleaning_Windows "Cleaning Windows")", that referenced one of Morrison's first jobs after leaving school.[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage337-338-147) Several other songs on the album, "[Vanlose Stairway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanlose_Stairway "Vanlose Stairway")", "She Gives Me Religion", and the instrumental, "[Scandinavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scandinavia_(composition) "Scandinavia (composition)")" show the presence of a new personal muse in his life: a Danish public relations agent, who would share Morrison's spiritual interests and serve as a steadying influence on him throughout most of the 1980s.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage371-148) "Scandinavia", with Morrison on piano,[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Inarticulate_Speech_of_the_Heart-149) was nominated in the _Best Rock Instrumental Performance_ category for the 25th Annual [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards").[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-150)

Much of the music Morrison released throughout the 1980s continued to focus on the themes of [spirituality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirituality "Spirituality") and faith. His 1983 album, _[Inarticulate Speech of the Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inarticulate\_Speech\_of\_the\_Heart "Inarticulate Speech of the Heart")_, was "a move towards creating music for meditation" with synthesisers, uilleann pipes and flute sounds, and four of the tracks were instrumentals.[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage153-151) The titling of the album and the presence of the instrumentals were noted to be indicative of Morrison's long-held belief that "it's not the words one uses but the force of conviction behind those words that matters."[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Inarticulate_Speech_of_the_Heart-149) During this period of time, Morrison had studied [Scientology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientology "Scientology") and gave "Special Thanks" to [L. Ron Hubbard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L._Ron_Hubbard "L. Ron Hubbard") on the album's credits.[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage150-152)

_[A Sense of Wonder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Sense\_of\_Wonder "A Sense of Wonder")_, Morrison's 1985 album, pulled together the spiritual themes contained in his last four albums, which were defined in a _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling\_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ review as: "rebirth (_Into the Music_), deep contemplation and meditation (_Common One_); ecstasy and humility (_Beautiful Vision_); and blissful, mantra like languor (_Inarticulate Speech of the Heart_)."[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-A_Sense_of_Wonder-153) The single "[Tore Down a la Rimbaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tore_Down_a_la_Rimbaud "Tore Down a la Rimbaud")" was a reference to [Rimbaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Rimbaud "Arthur Rimbaud") and an earlier bout of [writer's block](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writer's_block "Writer's block") that Morrison had encountered in 1974.[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage308-154) In 1985, Morrison also wrote the musical score for the movie _[Lamb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamb\_(1985\_film) "Lamb (1985 film)")_ starring [Liam Neeson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liam_Neeson "Liam Neeson").[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-CollisPage162-155)

Morrison's 1986 release, _[No Guru, No Method, No Teacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No\_Guru,\_No\_Method,\_No\_Teacher "No Guru, No Method, No Teacher")_, was said to contain a "genuine holiness ... and musical freshness that needs to be set in context to understand."[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage255-156) Critical response was favourable with a _Sounds_ reviewer calling the album "his most intriguingly involved since _Astral Weeks_" and "Morrison at his most mystical, magical best."[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage396-157)[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage360-158) It contains the song "[In the Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In_the_Garden_(Van_Morrison_song) "In the Garden (Van Morrison song)")" that, according to Morrison, had a "definite meditation process which is a 'form' of transcendental meditation as its basis. It's not TM".[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage255-156) He entitled the album as a rebuttal to media attempts to place him in various creeds.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage253-159) In an interview in the Observer he told Anthony Denselow:

> There have been many lies put out about me and this finally states my position. I have never joined any organisation, nor plan to. I am not affiliated to any guru, don't subscribe to any method and for those people who don't know what a guru is, I don't have a teacher either.[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage253-254-160)

After releasing the "No Guru" album, Morrison's music appeared less gritty and more [adult contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_contemporary_music "Adult contemporary music") with the well-received 1987 album, _[Poetic Champions Compose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetic\_Champions\_Compose "Poetic Champions Compose")_, considered to be one of his recording highlights of the 1980s.[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-161) The romantic ballad from this album, "[Someone Like You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Someone_Like_You_(Van_Morrison_song) "Someone Like You (Van Morrison song)")", has been featured subsequently in the soundtracks of several movies, including 1995's _[French Kiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_Kiss\_(1995\_film) "French Kiss (1995 film)")_, and in 2001, both _[Someone Like You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Someone\_like\_You\_(2001\_film) "Someone like You (2001 film)")_ and _[Bridget Jones's Diary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridget\_Jones's\_Diary\_(film) "Bridget Jones's Diary (film)")_.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Van_Morrison_at_IMDb-141)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-162)

In 1988, he released _[Irish Heartbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish\_Heartbeat "Irish Heartbeat")_, a collection of traditional [Irish folk songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folk_music_of_Ireland "Folk music of Ireland") recorded with the Irish group [the Chieftains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Chieftains "The Chieftains"), which reached number 18 in the UK album charts. The title song, "[Irish Heartbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Heartbeat_(song) "Irish Heartbeat (song)")", was originally recorded on his 1983 album _Inarticulate Speech of the Heart_.[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-163)

The 1989 album, _[Avalon Sunset](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalon\_Sunset "Avalon Sunset")_, which featured the hit duet with [Cliff Richard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cliff_Richard "Cliff Richard") "[Whenever God Shines His Light](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whenever_God_Shines_His_Light "Whenever God Shines His Light")" and the ballad "[Have I Told You Lately](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Have_I_Told_You_Lately "Have I Told You Lately")" (on which "earthly love transmutes into that for God" ([Hinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Hinton "Brian Hinton"))),[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage278-164) reached 13 on the UK album chart. Although considered to be a deeply spiritual album,[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-165) it also contained "Daring Night", which "deals with full, blazing sex, whatever its churchy organ and gentle lilt suggest"(Hinton).[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HintonPage280-166) Morrison's familiar themes of "God, woman, his childhood in Belfast and those enchanted moments when time stands still" were prominent in the songs.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage163-167) He can be heard calling out the change of [tempo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tempo "Tempo") at the end of this song, repeating the numbers "1–4" to cue the [chord changes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chord_progression "Chord progression") (the first and fourth chord in the key of the music). He often completed albums in two days, frequently releasing first takes.[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-168)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage429-463-169)

### _The Best of Van Morrison_ to _Back on Top_: 1990–1999

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: The Best of Van Morrison to Back on Top: 1990–1999")]

The early to middle 1990s were commercially successful for Morrison with three albums reaching the top five of the UK charts, sold-out concerts, and a more visible public profile; but this period also marked a decline in the critical reception to his work.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage450-458-170) The decade began with the release of _[The Best of Van Morrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Best\_of\_Van\_Morrison "The Best of Van Morrison")_; compiled by Morrison himself, the album was focused on his hit singles, and became a multi-platinum success remaining a year and a half on the UK charts. [AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") determined it to be "far and away the best-selling album of his career."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-allmusic_Biography:_Van_Morrison-110)[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-171) In 1991 he wrote and produced four songs for [Tom Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Jones_(singer) "Tom Jones (singer)") released on the _Carrying A Torch_ album and performed a duet with [Bob Dylan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan") on BBC Arena special.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-:02-172)

The 1994 live double album _[A Night in San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Night\_in\_San\_Francisco "A Night in San Francisco")_ received favourable reviews as well as commercial success by reaching number eight on the UK charts.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-ANISF-173)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-174)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-175)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-176) 1995's _[Days Like This](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Days\_Like\_This\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Days Like This (Van Morrison album)")_ also had large sales—though the critical reviews were not always favourable.[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Heylin_Page458-177) This period also saw a number of side projects, including the live jazz performances of 1996's _[How Long Has This Been Going On](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How\_Long\_Has\_This\_Been\_Going\_On\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "How Long Has This Been Going On (Van Morrison album)")_, from the same year _[Tell Me Something: The Songs of Mose Allison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tell\_Me\_Something:\_The\_Songs\_of\_Mose\_Allison "Tell Me Something: The Songs of Mose Allison")_, and 2000's _[The Skiffle Sessions – Live in Belfast 1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Skiffle\_Sessions\_%E2%80%93\_Live\_in\_Belfast\_1998 "The Skiffle Sessions – Live in Belfast 1998")_, all of which found Morrison paying tribute to his early musical influences.

In 1997, Morrison released _[The Healing Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Healing\_Game "The Healing Game")_. The album received mixed reviews, with the lyrics being described as "tired" and "dull",[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-RoganPage450-178) though critic Greil Marcus praised the musical complexity of the album by saying: "It carries the listener into a musical home so perfect and complete he or she might have forgotten that music could call up such a place, and then populate it with people, acts, wishes, fears."[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-MarcusPage111-179) The following year, Morrison finally released some of his previously unissued studio recordings in a two-disc set, _[The Philosopher's Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Philosopher's\_Stone\_(album) "The Philosopher's Stone (album)")_. His next release, 1999's _[Back on Top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back\_on\_Top\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Back on Top (Van Morrison album)")_, achieved modest success, being his highest-charting album in the US since 1978's _[Wavelength](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavelength\_(album) "Wavelength (album)")_.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-180)

### _Down the Road_ to _Keep It Simple_: 2000–2009

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Down the Road to Keep It Simple: 2000–2009")]

Van Morrison continued to record and tour in the 2000s, often performing two or three times a week.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-concerts-181) He formed his own independent label, Exile Productions Ltd, which enables him to maintain full production control of each album he records, which he then delivers as a finished product to the recording label that he chooses, for marketing and distribution.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-CollisPage181-182)

In 2001, nine months into a tour with [Linda Gail Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linda_Gail_Lewis "Linda Gail Lewis") promoting their collaboration _[You Win Again](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You\_Win\_Again\_(album) "You Win Again (album)")_, Lewis left the tour, later filing claims against Morrison for unfair dismissal and sexual discrimination. Both claims were later withdrawn, and Morrison's solicitor said, "(Mr Morrison's) pleased that these claims have finally been withdrawn. He accepted a full apology and comprehensive retraction which represents a complete vindication of his stance from the outset. Miss Lewis has given a full and categorical apology and retraction to Mr Morrison." Lewis' legal representative Christine Thompson said both parties had agreed to the terms of the settlement.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-autogenerated1-183)

The album _[Down the Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down\_the\_Road\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Down the Road (Van Morrison album)")_, released in May 2002, received a good critical reception and proved to be his highest-charting album in the US since 1972's _Saint Dominic's Preview_.[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Charts_&_Awards-125) It had a nostalgic tone, with its fifteen tracks representing the various musical genres Morrison had previously covered—including R&B, blues, country and folk;[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-184) one of the tracks was written as a tribute to his late father George, who had played a pivotal role in nurturing his early musical tastes.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-TurnerPage20-20)

Morrison's 2005 album, _[Magic Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic\_Time\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Magic Time (Van Morrison album)")_, debuted at number twenty-five on the US [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200") charts upon its May release, some forty years after Morrison first entered the public's eye as the frontman of Them. _Rolling Stone_ listed it as number seventeen on _The Top 50 Records of 2005_.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-185) Also in July 2005, Morrison was named by [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon.com "Amazon.com") as one of their top twenty-five all-time best-selling artists and inducted into the Amazon.com Hall of Fame.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-186) Later in the year, Morrison also donated a previously unreleased studio track to a charity album, _[Hurricane Relief: Come Together Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane\_Relief:\_Come\_Together\_Now "Hurricane Relief: Come Together Now")_, which raised money for relief efforts intended for [Gulf Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Coast_of_the_United_States "Gulf Coast of the United States") victims devastated by hurricanes [Katrina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Katrina "Hurricane Katrina") and [Rita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Rita "Hurricane Rita").[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-187) Morrison composed the song, "Blue and Green", featuring [Foggy Lyttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foggy_Lyttle "Foggy Lyttle") on guitar. This song was released in 2007 on the album, _[The Best of Van Morrison Volume 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Best\_of\_Van\_Morrison\_Volume\_3 "The Best of Van Morrison Volume 3")_ and also as a single in the UK. Van Morrison was a headline act at the international Celtic music festival, The [Hebridean Celtic Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebridean_Celtic_Festival "Hebridean Celtic Festival") in [Stornoway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stornoway "Stornoway"), Outer Hebrides in the summer of 2005.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-188)

He released an album with a country music theme, entitled _[Pay the Devil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pay\_the\_Devil "Pay the Devil")_, on 7 March 2006 and appeared at the [Ryman Auditorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryman_Auditorium "Ryman Auditorium"), where the tickets sold out immediately after they went on sale.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-189)_Pay the Devil_ debuted at number twenty-six on the Billboard 200 and peaked at number seven on Top Country Albums.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-190)[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-191) Amazon Best of 2006 Editor's Picks in Country listed the country album at number ten in December 2006. Still promoting the country album, Morrison's performance as the headline act on the first night of the [Austin City Limits Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austin_City_Limits_Music_Festival "Austin City Limits Music Festival") on 15 September 2006 was reviewed by _Rolling Stone_ magazine as one of the top ten shows of the 2006 festival.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-ACL2006-192) In November 2006, a limited edition album, _[Live at Austin City Limits Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_at\_Austin\_City\_Limits\_Festival "Live at Austin City Limits Festival")_, was issued by Exile Productions, Ltd. A later deluxe CD/DVD release of _Pay the Devil_, in the summer of 2006, contained tracks from the Ryman performance.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-193) In October 2006, Morrison had released his first commercial DVD, _[Live at Montreux 1980/1974](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live\_at\_Montreux\_1980/1974 "Live at Montreux 1980/1974")_, with concerts taken from two separate appearances at the [Montreux Jazz Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreux_Jazz_Festival "Montreux Jazz Festival").

A new double CD [compilation album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compilation_album "Compilation album"), _[The Best of Van Morrison Volume 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Best\_of\_Van\_Morrison\_Volume\_3 "The Best of Van Morrison Volume 3")_, was released in June 2007 containing thirty-one tracks, some of which were previously unreleased. Morrison selected the tracks, which ranged from the 1993 album _Too Long in Exile_ to the song "[Stranded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stranded_(Van_Morrison_song) "Stranded (Van Morrison song)")" from the 2005 album _Magic Time_.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-194) On 3 September 2007, Morrison's complete catalogue of albums from 1971 through 2002 were made available exclusively at the [iTunes Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITunes_Store "ITunes Store") in Europe and Australia and during the first week of October 2007, the albums became available at the US iTunes Store.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-195)

_[Still on Top – The Greatest Hits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Still\_on\_Top\_%E2%80%93\_The\_Greatest\_Hits "Still on Top – The Greatest Hits")_, a thirty-seven-track double CD compilation album, was released on 22 October 2007 in the UK on the Polydor label. On 29 October 2007, the album charted at number two on the Official UK Top 75 Albums—his highest UK charting.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-196) The November release in the US and Canada contains twenty-one selected tracks.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-197) The hits released on albums with the copyrights owned by Morrison as Exile Productions Ltd.—1971 and later—had been remastered in 2007.

_[Keep It Simple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep\_It\_Simple "Keep It Simple")_, Morrison's 33rd studio album of completely new material, was released by Exile/Polydor Records on 17 March 2008 in the UK and released by Exile/[Lost Highway Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lost_Highway_Records "Lost Highway Records") in the US and Canada on 1 April 2008.[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-198) It comprised eleven self-penned tracks. Morrison promoted the album with a short US tour including an appearance at the [SXSW](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_by_Southwest "South by Southwest") music conference,[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-199)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-200) and a UK concert broadcast on [BBC Radio 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_2 "BBC Radio 2"). In the first week of release _Keep It Simple_ debuted on the Billboard 200 chart at number ten, Morrison's first Top Ten charting in the US.[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-201)

### _Born to Sing_ to _Three Chords_: 2010–2020

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Born to Sing to Three Chords: 2010–2020")]

Morrison released two albums in the first half of the decade, followed by a further six in just five years, his productivity increasing noticeably as he turned 70. _[Born to Sing: No Plan B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born\_to\_Sing:\_No\_Plan\_B "Born to Sing: No Plan B")_ was released on 2 October 2012 on [Blue Note Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Note_Records "Blue Note Records"). The album was recorded in [Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast "Belfast"), Morrison's birthplace and hometown.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-202) The first single from this album, "Open the Door (To Your Heart)", was released on 24 August 2012.[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-203) A selection of Morrison's lyrics, _Lit Up Inside_, was published by [City Lights Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Lights_Books "City Lights Books") in the US and [Faber & Faber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faber_&_Faber "Faber & Faber") in the UK.[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-204) The book was released on 2 October 2014 and an evening of words and music commenced at the Lyric Theatre, London on 17 November 2014 to mark its launch. Morrison himself selected his best and most iconic lyrics from a catalog of 50 years of writing.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-205)

In 2015, Morrison sold the rights to most of his catalogue to [Legacy Recordings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legacy_Recordings "Legacy Recordings"), the catalog division of [Sony Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Music "Sony Music"). This resulted in 33 of his albums being made available as digital releases and through all streaming services for the first time that August.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-206) His first album recorded with Sony under the new contract was _[Duets: Re-working the Catalogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duets:\_Re-working\_the\_Catalogue "Duets: Re-working the Catalogue")_, released on 24 March 2015 on the subsidiary, [RCA Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Records "RCA Records").[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-207) Morrison's 70th birthday in 2015 was marked by celebrations in his hometown of Belfast, commencing with [BBC Radio Ulster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Radio_Ulster "BBC Radio Ulster") presenting programs including "Top 70 Van Tracks" between 26 and 28 August. As the headline act ending the Eastside Arts Festival, Morrison performed two 70th-birthday concerts on [Cyprus Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus_Avenue "Cyprus Avenue") on his birthday 31 August. The first of the concerts was broadcast live on BBC Radio Ulster and a 60-minute BBC film of highlights from the concerts, entitled _Up On Cyprus Avenue_, was first shown on 4 September.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-208)[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-209)[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-eastside_arts_fest-210)[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Thousands_attend-211) The following year, on 30 September, Morrison released _[Keep Me Singing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keep\_Me\_Singing "Keep Me Singing")_, his 36th studio album. "Too Late", the first single, was released on the same day. The songs are twelve originals and one cover and the album represents his first release of originals since _Born to Sing: No Plan B_ in 2012. A short tour of the U.S. followed with six dates in October 2016,[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Keep_Me_Singing-212) followed by a short tour of the U.K. with eight dates in October—December 2016, including a London show at _[The O2 Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_O2\_Arena "The O2 Arena")_ on 30 October. The U.S. tour resumed in January 2017 with five new dates in [Las Vegas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas "Las Vegas") and [Clearwater, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clearwater,_Florida "Clearwater, Florida").[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-213)

Morrison's album _[Roll with the Punches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roll\_with\_the\_Punches\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Roll with the Punches (Van Morrison album)")_ was released on 22 September 2017. That July, he and Universal Music Group were sued by former professional wrestler [Billy Two Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Two_Rivers "Billy Two Rivers") for using his likeness on its cover and promotional material without his permission. On 4 August, Two Rivers' lawyer said the parties had reached a preliminary agreement to settle the matter out of court.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-214) He released his 38th studio album, _[Versatile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versatile\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Versatile (Van Morrison album)")_, on 1 December 2017. It features covers of nine classic jazz standards and seven original songs including his arrangement of the traditional "Skye Boat Song".[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Van_Morrison_'versatile'-215) He quickly followed up with his 39th studio album, _[You're Driving Me Crazy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/You're\_Driving\_Me\_Crazy\_(album) "You're Driving Me Crazy (album)")_, released on 27 April 2018 via Sony Legacy Recordings. The album features a collaboration with [Joey DeFrancesco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joey_DeFrancesco "Joey DeFrancesco") on a mixture of blues and jazz classics that include eight Morrison originals from his back catalogue.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-216)

In October 2018, Morrison announced that his 40th studio album, _[The Prophet Speaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Prophet\_Speaks "The Prophet Speaks")_, would be released by Caroline International on 7 December 2018.[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-217) A year later, in November 2019, he released his 41st studio album, _[Three Chords & the Truth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three\_Chords\_&\_the\_Truth\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Three Chords & the Truth (Van Morrison album)")_. On 5 March 2020 [Faber and Faber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faber_and_Faber "Faber and Faber") published _Keep 'Er Lit_, the second volume of Van Morrison's selected lyrics.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-218) It features a foreword of fellow poet [Paul Muldoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Muldoon "Paul Muldoon") and comprehends 120 songs from across his career.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-219) In November 2020 Morrison and [Eric Clapton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Clapton "Eric Clapton") collaborated on a single called "Stand and Deliver", whose profits from sales will be donated to Morrison's Lockdown Financial Hardship Fund.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-220)

### COVID-19 statements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: COVID-19 statements")]

During the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"), Morrison made numerous statements against [social distancing measures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_distancing_measures_related_to_the_COVID-19_pandemic "Social distancing measures related to the COVID-19 pandemic") that affected live music events, and made calls to "fight pseudo-science".[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-221) Continuing with this narrative, Morrison released three new songs in September 2020, which had messages of protest against [COVID-19 lockdowns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns") in the UK. Morrison accused the UK government of "taking our freedom".[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-:0-222) He had performed socially distanced concerts previously, but said that the shows were not a sign of "compliance".[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-223)

There were calls in Belfast for Belfast City Council to revoke his [Freedom of the City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_City "Freedom of the City") honour following the statements: city councillor Emmet McDonough-Brown said that his lyrics were "undermining the guidance in place to protect lives and are ignorant of established science as we grapple with Covid-19."[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-224) Northern Ireland health minister [Robin Swann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robin_Swann "Robin Swann") accused Morrison of smearing public health practitioners[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Swann-225) and called Morrison's anti-lockdown songs "dangerous".[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-:0-222) In November 2021, Swann sued Morrison for [defamation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defamation "Defamation"), after he said that Swann was a "fraud" and "very dangerous".[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-226)[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-227) In 2022, Morrison issued legal proceedings against Swann over an opinion piece in _Rolling Stone_ magazine that was critical of Morrison's anti-lockdown songs and actions.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-228) Both legal claims were settled confidentially shortly before their respective court proceedings were to begin in September 2024.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-229)

### 2020s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2020s")]

In March 2021, Morrison announced that his 42nd album, _[Latest Record Project, Volume 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latest\_Record\_Project,\_Volume\_1 "Latest Record Project, Volume 1")_, would be released by Exile Productions and [BMG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BMG_Rights_Management "BMG Rights Management") on 7 May. The 28-track album includes songs such as "Why Are You on Facebook?", "They Own The Media" and "Western Man". In addition to digitally, it was released as a 2-CD set and on triple vinyl.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-230)[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-231)[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-232) The album marked a return to the UK Top Ten for Morrison, making the 2020s the fourth consecutive decade in which he has achieved such success.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-233)

The following year, _[What's It Gonna Take?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/What's\_It\_Gonna\_Take%3F "What's It Gonna Take?")_ explored many of the same themes, but was less successful commercially.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-234) In 2023, he returned to his roots with _[Moving on Skiffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moving\_on\_Skiffle "Moving on Skiffle")_ and _[Accentuate the Positive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accentuate\_the\_Positive\_(Van\_Morrison\_album) "Accentuate the Positive (Van Morrison album)")_.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Uncut-235) He also issued archival material via his own direct-to-consumer label Orangefield Records, beginning with _Beyond Words: Instrumental_ and continuing in 2024 with _Live at Orangefield_, taken from a run of 2014 concerts at his former secondary school. His 2024 studio album _[New Arrangements and Duets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Arrangements\_and\_Duets "New Arrangements and Duets")_ also compiled unreleased material, including big band reworkings of songs from his catalogue and duets with [Kurt Elling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Elling "Kurt Elling"), [Curtis Stigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curtis_Stigers "Curtis Stigers"), [Joss Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joss_Stone "Joss Stone") and [Willie Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Nelson "Willie Nelson") recorded between 2014 and 2019.[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-The_Arts_Desk-236)

Van Morrison's songs were used extensively in [Kenneth Branagh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenneth_Branagh "Kenneth Branagh")'s Oscar-winning 2021 film _[Belfast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belfast\_(film) "Belfast (film)")_:[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-237) Morrison received his first nomination for the [Academy Award for Best Original Song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Original_Song "Academy Award for Best Original Song") for "Down to Joy".[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-238) Several tracks were also featured in _[Cherry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry\_(2021\_film) "Cherry (2021 film)")_, released the same year. "Down to Joy" would not be released on a Van Morrison album until 2025, when it became the lead single from _Remembering Now_, his first album of original material since 2022.

## Live performances

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Live performances")]

### 1970s

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Van_Morrison&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 1970s")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/VanMorrison_smiling.jpg/250px-VanMorrison_smiling.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:VanMorrison_smiling.jpg)

Morrison performing at the Marin Civic Center, 2007

By 1972, after being a performer for nearly ten years, Morrison began experiencing [stage fright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_fright "Stage fright") when performing for audiences of thousands, as opposed to the hundreds he had experienced in his early career. He became anxious on stage and had difficulty establishing eye contact with the audience. He once said in an interview about performing on stage, "I dig singing the songs but there are times when it's pretty agonising for me to be out there." After a brief break from music, he started appearing in clubs, regaining his ability to perform live, albeit with smaller audiences.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-Rolling_Stone_Interview-34)

The 1974 live double album _[It's Too Late to Stop Now](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_Too\_Late\_to\_Stop\_Now "It's Too Late to Stop Now")_ has been called one of the greatest recordings of a live concert[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-239)[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-240)[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-241) and has appeared on lists of greatest live albums of all time.[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-MOJO_Top_50_LIve_Albums-242)[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-243)[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-244)[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-245) Biographer [Johnny Rogan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Rogan "Johnny Rogan") wrote, "Morrison was in the midst of what was arguably his greatest phase as a performer."[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-246) Performances on the album were from tapes made during a three-month tour of the US and Europe in 1973 with the backing group [the Caledonia Soul Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Caledonia_Soul_Orchestra "The Caledonia Soul Orchestra"). Soon after recording the album, Morrison restructured the Caledonia Soul Orchestra into a smaller unit, the Caledonia Soul Express.[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_Morrison#cite_note-HeylinPage284-247)

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/The_Last_Waltz.jpg/250px-The_Last_Waltz.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Last_Waltz.jpg)

Morrison performs in 1976 at [the Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band")'s final concert filmed for _[The Last Waltz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Last\_Waltz "The Last Waltz")_.

On [Thanksgiving Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thanksgiving_(United_States) "Thanksgiving (United States)") 1976, Morrison performed at the farewell concert for [the Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Band "The Band"). It was his first live performance in several years, and he considered skipping his appearance until the last minute, even refusing to go on stage when they announced his name. Dolores Mary Eileen O'Riordan (/oʊˈrɪərdən/ oh-REER-dən; 6 September 1971 – 15 January 2018) was an Irish singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist who achieved international fame as the lead vocalist of the rock band the Cranberries.[2] O'Riordan was the principal songwriter of the band and also played acoustic and electric guitars. She became one of the most recognisable voices in alternative rock and was known for her lilting mezzo-soprano voice, signature yodel, use of keening, and strong Limerick accent.

O'Riordan was born in County Limerick, Ireland, to a Catholic working-class family. She began performing as a soloist in her church choir before leaving secondary school to join the Cranberries in 1990. The band released the number-one album Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We? in 1993; that album was followed by No Need to Argue (1994), To the Faithful Departed (1996), Bury the Hatchet (1999), and Wake Up and Smell the Coffee (2001). The Cranberries went on hiatus in 2003. During the hiatus, O'Riordan released two solo studio albums: Are You Listening? (2007) and No Baggage (2009). The Cranberries reunited in 2009,[3] released Roses (2012), and went on a world tour. O'Riordan's other activities included appearing as a judge on RTÉ's The Voice of Ireland (2013–2014) and recording material with the trio D.A.R.K. (2014). The Cranberries' seventh album, Something Else (2017), was the last to be released during her lifetime.

Throughout her life, O'Riordan suffered from depression and the pressure of her own success; she was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in 2015. O'Riordan died from drowning due to alcohol intoxication in January 2018 at the age of 46. After her death, the Cranberries released the Grammy-nominated album In the End (2019), which featured her final vocal recordings; the group then disbanded.[4] With the Cranberries, O'Riordan sold more than 40 million albums worldwide during her lifetime;[5] that total increased to almost 50 million albums worldwide as of 2019.[6] She was honoured with the Ivor Novello International Achievement award. In the months following her death, O'Riordan was named "The Top Female Artist of All Time" on Billboard's Alternative Songs chart.

Early life and educationedit

Dolores Mary Eileen O'Riordan was born on 6 September 1971 in Ballybricken in County Limerick, Ireland,[7] the youngest of nine children, two of whom died in infancy.[8] Her father, Terence Patrick "Terry" O'Riordan (1937–2011),[9] worked as a farm labourer until a motorbike accident in 1968 left him brain damaged.[10] Her mother, Eileen (née Greensmith), was a school caterer.[8] O'Riordan was raised in a devout Roman Catholic family,[11] and was named by her mother in reference to the Lady of the Seven Dolours.[12][13]

O'Riordan was singing before she could talk.[14] When she was five years of age, the principal of her school took her into the sixth class, sat her on the teacher's desk, and told her to sing for the twelve-year-old students in the class.[15][16] She started with traditional Irish music[16] and playing the Irish tin whistle when she went to school.[17][18]

When O'Riordan was seven years old, her sister accidentally burned the family house down.[19][20] The family's rural community was able to raise funds to purchase a new homestead for them.[19] O'Riordan's formative experiences were as a liturgical soloist in the choir in a local church and as a singer at school.[18][21] From the age of eight, she was sexually abused for four years by a person whom she trusted.[22][23] At the age of ten, she sang in local pubs where her uncles took her.[18][24]

O'Riordan attended Laurel Hill Coláiste FCJ school in Limerick.[7][25] School principal Aedín Ní Bhriain said in the Limerick Post about O'Riordan's first day at Laurel Hill Coláiste at the age of twelve that she stood up in front of classmates and announced: "My name is Dolores O'Riordan and I'm going to be a rock star". She then stood on her chair and sang "Tra la la la la, Triangle".[21][26] According to her school friend Catherina Egan, she was "boisterous, wild, but lovely".[21][26] She regularly played the spoons and the bodhrán.[17] At the age of twelve, O'Riordan began piano lessons, and then later, achieved Grade 4 in Practical and Grade 8 in Theory.[17][18] She sat every day at the piano in the main hall to play, then her classmates sat around her after having lunch to listen to her sing.[21][26] At age 17, she learned to play the guitar and performed a solo gig in Laurel Hill Coláiste secondary school.[27] That same year, she met her first boyfriend, Mike O'Mahoney.[28][29]

She described having a strict daily routine through her teenage years that consisted of going to piano lessons, going to church and doing homework.[30] O'Riordan later admitted that she had neglected her school lessons in favour of writing music and songs, although at school she became head girl.[21][31] Former principal Anne Mordan said in Nova about O'Riordan that she was a "delightful, unsophisticated, sensitive student, who enjoyed her time with us"; she described her as "a bright, kind, good-humoured girl, who loved her family, her friends, and had an easy relationship with all her teachers, both lay and FCJ sisters."[32] During her six years at Laurel Hill Coláiste, O'Riordan won the Slógadh song contest almost every year,[21][33] at several local events, and culminating in national singing competitions.[18][33] In total she won 20 Slógadh medals.[34]

Around this time, O'Riordan divided the rest of her schedule among assisting her mother, learning the accordion from her dad, and having part-time employment at clothing shops.[35] Her mother, whom she "adored", encouraged her to consider becoming a nun or get a college degree and become a music teacher; instead, she ran away from home at 18 and lived a couple of years with her boyfriend.[36][37][38] In an interview with Vox magazine, O'Riordan clarified her reasons for leaving home: "At 18 I left home because I wanted to sing. My parents wanted me to go to college and things like that. I was really poor for a year-and-a-half; I remember actually being hungry, like I'd die for a bag of chips. That's when I joined the Cranberries".[39]

Careeredit
1989–2003: Formation of the Cranberries, early success and stardomedit
Main article: The Cranberries

In 1989, brothers Mike (bass) and Noel (guitar) Hogan formed the Cranberry Saw Us with drummer Fergal Lawler and singer Niall Quinn, in Limerick, Ireland.[40][41] Less than a year later, Quinn left the band.[42][43][a] He then told the remaining members that his girlfriend knew a girl who was looking for a band playing original material.[16][44]

In mid-1990, on a Sunday afternoon, O'Riordan and Quinn came to the band's rehearsal room. Noel Hogan later recalled that "Niall came up with Dolores on that Sunday and I remember she was shy, very soft-spoken. Not the Dolores that everyone grew to know. And she comes in and we're just kind of a gang of young guys sitting around the place. It must have been very, very intimidating for her".[44] O'Riordan sang a couple of songs that she had written and she also did a Sinéad O'Connor song, "Troy".[44] The band was impressed and gave her a cassette with instrumentals, asking her if she could work on it.[16][20] When she returned with a rough version of "Linger", she was hired.[16][45] Hogan told Rolling Stone that "the minute she sang, you know, it was like your jaw drops at her voice. Dolores was musically far superior to me, because she had been doing it all her life".[44]

O'Riordan was still a student at Laurel Hill Coláiste FCJ secondary school when she first joined the band.[34][46] She had set her sights on the musical life and her desire to be in "a band with no barriers, where I could write my own songs", she told The Guardian in 1995.[8] At the time, she was doing her Leaving Certificate.[7] Although her marks in school were good, academic study did not hold much interest for her.[16] As a result, she left school without any qualifications.[31]

The group recorded demo tapes, including Nothing Left at All, a three-track EP released on tape by local record label Xeric Records which sold 300 copies.[20][47] The owner of Xeric Studios, Pearse Gilmore, became their manager and provided the group with studio time to complete another demo tape, which he produced.[16] It featured early versions of "Linger" and "Dreams", which were sent to record companies in the UK.[48] This demo gained attention from both the UK press and the record industry and sparked a bidding war among record labels.[16][49] Eventually, the group signed with Island Records.[16][50] The group changed their name to "the Cranberries" and released a four-track EP, Uncertain.[20][45]

By then, O'Riordan was experiencing difficult touring conditions with low income, sleeping on people's floors and in cramped vans across Ireland and the UK.[16][47] Furthermore, she had to overcome her shyness; during her early live performances with the Cranberries, she sang "with her back to the audience".[47][51] Lawler recalled, "we just went up, and we had six songs. Dolores was turned to the side; Noel, Mike and I had our heads down".[16][47] At this stage, she had spent eight years with classical piano, and had played the harmonium in her church for ten years.[17][30] O'Riordan rapidly gained international attention after the release of the Cranberries' first album, Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We?.[8][49] It contained the group's most successful singles, "Dreams" and "Linger", which charted at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 when she was only 22.[52]

Early in 1994, O'Riordan injured her cruciate ligament in a ski accident in the Alps' Val-d'Isère and underwent major surgery.[8][53] In September 1994, the Cranberries released "Zombie", the lead single of the follow-up album, No Need To Argue.[54] The song reached No. 1 on Triple J's Hottest 100, which was the first time ever that a female-led band had topped Australia's biggest song poll.[55][56] She stood alone in the countdown's history for 16 years.[55] In terms of female-fronted acts, as of 2024, O'Riordan remains one of only four women to sing on a No. 1 song on the Hottest 100 ranking.[55][b] The Cranberries reached their commercial peak with No Need to Argue, the top-selling album worldwide in the first half of 1995[58] and the world's best-selling album of the year by a European artist.[59] The album produced the songs "Ode to My Family", "I Can't Be with You", "Ridiculous Thoughts" and the group's biggest international hit, "Zombie", which topped singles charts in several countries.[60] Dan Weiss of Billboard stated that "Zombie" "could crush an entire room with the combined largesse of O'Riordan's ocean-swallowing voice".[61] By this time, O'Riordan had achieved both success and celebrity status.[62]

O'Riordan's leg injury recurred unexpectedly and led to cancellation of the three concerts scheduled in Ireland for December 1994.[53] This resulted in a press backlash, while the audience was more understanding, as O'Riordan had mentioned that the concerts were not cancelled but postponed until June 1995.[53]

O'Riordan was recognised as a style icon. In the 1990s, she sported a pixie cut or buzzed hair and performing barefoot, saying that "it just feels comfortable and honest to pull your toes along the ground".[8][63][64] Billboard's William Goodman described O'Riordan performing "Barefoot and strutting onstage, an Irish warrior poet with a bleached blonde pixie cut, gold chain necklace, singing without a flinch, as if it were ordained".[5] The New York Times mentioned that O'Riordan was responsible for a large portion of Dr. Martens boots sales in the 1990s.[62]

After attending a concert of the Cranberries at London's Royal Albert Hall in January 1995, author Alec Foege described O'Riordan as "part Audrey Hepburn, part David Bowie".[16] On 23 March 1995, O'Riordan appeared on the cover of Rolling Stone magazine.[65] On 12 September 1995, O'Riordan performed "Ave Maria" along with Luciano Pavarotti in his Pavarotti & Friends series of benefit concerts, entitled Together for the Children of Bosnia, which raised funds for War Child and the children of Bosnia, held in Modena, Italy.[66] Princess Diana, who attended the live performance, told O'Riordan that the song brought her to tears.[67] During the show, O'Riordan performed "Linger" as a duet with Simon Le Bon of Duran Duran.[68]

The Cranberries' third album, To the Faithful Departed debuted at number two in the UK,[69] and number four in the US,[70] with the singles "Free to Decide", "When You're Gone" and "Hollywood".[69] It also featured the Billboard Modern Rock Tracks number-one single "Salvation".[69] Halfway through the Free To Decide World Tour 1996–97 promoting To the Faithful Departed, O'Riordan and the Cranberries canceled the remaining dates and announced that they would take time off in 1997.[29][66] O'Riordan publicly told the Irish Examiner, "I was very depressed and I was extremely anorexic on that record, and as it came out I got progressively worse".[71] O'Riordan was the one who made the decision to take a break;[29] although their management and record company "went mental", the rest of the group supported her.[72] Stephen Street later said that "perhaps she could have tempered her behavior and been more measured, but that wasn't her way."[51]

On 12 November 1998, O'Riordan and Fergal Lawler presented the award for Best Song at the MTV Europe Music Awards, in Milan, Italy.[73][74] On 11 December 1998, she performed live with the Cranberries at the Nobel Peace Prize Concert at Oslo Spektrum, Oslo, Norway.[66]

The Cranberries released Bury the Hatchet in 1999.[59][65] The album peaked at number one on both the Canadian Albums Chart[75] and on the European Top 100 Albums,[76] but did not match the commercial success of the group's first two albums.[59] The world tour supporting the album, which started in April 1999 and lasted until July 2000, was the band's biggest tour ever.[29][69]

O'Riordan in 2001

Bury the Hatchet was quickly followed by O'Riordan's fifth effort with the group, Wake Up and Smell the Coffee. The album was released on 22 October 2001.[59][65] On 15 December 2001, O'Riordan performed solo in the Vatican as part of the annual Vatican Christmas concert (Concerto di Natale) for Pope John Paul II.[77][78] She sang "Analyse", "Panis angelicus", "Little Drummer Boy" and "Silent Night" with a 67-piece orchestra.[77] The show was broadcast to well over 200 million people around the world.[79][80][81]

On 7 February 2002, O'Riordan and the Cranberries announced in Dublin that they had donated all the proceeds from their single "Time Is Ticking Out" to the Chernobyl Children's Project.[82][83] She was accompanied at the Clarence Hotel by Ali Hewson and by the founder and executive director of the Chernobyl Children's Project, Adi Roche. O'Riordan had written the song in spring 2001 after seeing images shared with her by Hewson and Roche of children born with congenital anomalies and illnesses caused by the Chernobyl nuclear disaster of 26 April 1986.[82][83] O'Riordan explained, "I had just given birth to my second child, a beautiful healthy little girl. [ ... ] I had spoken with Ali on the subject before this, but I was so moved, almost to tears, that I wrote "Time Is Ticking Out"".[82][83] On 14 December 2002 she received a second invitation to perform at the Vatican Christmas concert.[78] O'Riordan sang "Linger", "Happy Xmas (War Is Over)" and "Adeste Fideles". Dolores was supported by the Millennium Symphony Orchestra on the three songs, directed by Renato Serio, and also by the Summertime Gospel Choir on "Adeste Fideles".[79][84][85]

In June 2003, O'Riordan met AC/DC singer Brian Johnson when the Cranberries were playing concerts with AC/DC and the Rolling Stones on the latest leg of their Licks World Tour, and they considered the idea of working together.[86][87] In mid-July 2003, the two friends started collaborating on material for a project that was intended to be the rock opera version of Helen Of Troy, complete with "rousing anthems, tender ballads and minimal dialogue".[88][89] Johnson said he had been working on the project for about seven years and that the musical was expected to feature many artists.[88] The $1.2 million production was initially to debut in March 2003 at the Van Wezel Performing Arts Hall in Florida.[88] However, despite the pronouncement, the project was put on hold.[88]

2003–2009: Solo career and other projectsedit
O'Riordan on stage during a soundcheck at Festivalbar in Italy in May 2004

In 2003, the Cranberries decided to take a temporary time-out to experiment with solo projects.[90] O'Riordan stated that she had become a prisoner of her own celebrity and could not find a balance in her life.[91] In The Independent, O'Riordan said she needed time not only to focus on her family and health, but also on her solo career.[92]

In 2003, O'Riordan recruited Canadian music producer Dan Brodbeck and musicians to develop new compositions for a solo project.[93] Among them was drummer Graham Hopkins, whom O'Riordan said she "loved for his energy".[93] Also included were bassist Marco Mendoza, who had been a long time friend of O'Riordan and her husband; while Mendoza's father was a good friend of O'Riordan's father-in-law,[93] as well as Steve DeMarchi as the main guitarist, who used to do live sessions with the Cranberries, along with his brother Denny DeMarchi who played keyboards and guitars for the band in the early 2000s.[93] Brodbeck stated that their hiring was "100 per cent based on personalities clicking and musical tastes".[94][95] The DeMarchi brothers' family had long been friends with Dolores O'Riordan's husband and their three children.[94] In a Canadian newspaper, Denny DeMarchi said that she was "a perfectionist on tour"; occasionally during the show, she would turn to her musicians and canceled a particular song "in the moment".[94][95] Although the technical crew was frustrated because they had to make various changes, understanding prevailed, saying that "she was emotionally not able to go there". As described by DeMarchi, "[f]or her, singing wasn't just something to deliver... it was a real experience."[94][95]

"The Woodstrip / There's No Way Out"
"The Woodstrip / There's No Way Out" (2004), written by O'Riordan and Angelo Badalamenti, showcases part of her wide spectrum of musical expression.[96][97]

Sample of "Mirror Lover" (2005), a collaboration between Dolores O'Riordan and Jam & Spoon.
