On 6 March 2004, O'Riordan performed "Ave Maria" during the 54th International Song Festival at the Ariston Theater, Sanremo, in northern Italy.[98] On 29 May 2004, O'Riordan performed during the first concert of the Festivalbar, in Milan, Italy.[99] In 2004, she appeared with the Italian artist Zucchero on the album Zu & Co., with the song "Pure Love".[100][101] In 2004, O'Riordan worked with composer Angelo Badalamenti of Twin Peaks fame on the Evilenko soundtrack, providing vocals on several tracks, including "Angels Go to Heaven", the film's theme song.[102][103][104] Badalamenti later said that "she's a wonderful lyricist with an edge to her voice".[105]

In 2005, she appeared on the Jam & Spoon's album Tripomatic Fairytales 3003 as a guest vocalist on the track "Mirror Lover".[96][106] On 3 December 2005, O'Riordan made her third appearance at the Vatican's annual Christmas concert, where she performed "War Is Over", "Linger" and "Adeste Fideles" in a duet with Italian tenor Gian Luca Terranova.[79]

In April 2006, O'Riordan signed a contract with Ciulla Management, based in Sherman Oaks, California.[107][108] Prematurely before the release of her first solo album, the former Trent Reznor and Marilyn Manson mentor Tony Ciulla became her manager.[107][108] She made a cameo appearance in the Adam Sandler comedy Click, released on 23 June 2006, as a wedding singer performing an alternate version of the Cranberries' "Linger", set to strings.[96][107] On 9 December 2006, she would be invited at the Vatican Christmas concert which took place in Monte Carlo, as the concert which was to be held at the Vatican was canceled by the Pope Benedict XVI.[109] She sang "Angel Fire" from her forthcoming solo album with an orchestra and Steve DeMarchi, along with "Away in a Manger" and "Happy Xmas (War Is Over)".[79] In December 2006, Sanctuary Records signed O'Riordan for a solo record deal; of their recently signed artist, Julian Wall of Sanctuary Records noted that "Dolores comes to us with an immense international CV".[110][111]

The music video for "Ordinary Day", directed by Caswell Coggins, was filmed in Prague, in February 2007.[112][113] Are You Listening? was released in May 2007. The album entered and peaked at number 23 on the Billboard Top Rock Albums ranking, and number 77 on the Billboard 200.[60] "Ordinary Day" was its first single, released in late April, and was produced by Martin "Youth" Glover.[114] In August, "When We Were Young" was released as the second single from the album.[115] Colm O'Hare of Hot Press averred that O'Riordan could have chosen to exploit the underlying sonorities of the Cranberries on Are you Listening? to keep her devotees waiting until the reunion, but instead, "she's done something far more ambitious by releasing this multi-layered collection of songs that traverses styles and genres".[116] At that time, the couple split their time between Dublin and her husband's native Canada "surrounded by bears, wolves and all that great outdoor stuff", said O'Riordan.[117]

O'Riordan performed live on television many times in 2007 in support of Are You Listening?. She travelled to over 22 countries in Europe, North America and South America on the 2007 O'Riordan world tour.[111][118] On 21 March 2007, she performed on TV show Taratata in Paris, France.[119] On 20 April 2007, O'Riordan made an appearance live on The Late Late Show on RTÉ in Dublin.[120] On 16 May 2007, she appeared on Carson Daly's late-night show, Last Call with Carson Daly, in Burbank, California, in an episode that aired on 18 May 2007.[111][121] She also appeared on 17 May 2007, on NBC's The Tonight Show with Jay Leno in Burbank, California, in an episode that aired on 19 May 2007.[111][122] On 25 May 2007, O'Riordan performed during a live broadcast of Channel 7's Sunrise in Sydney, Australia.[123] In May 2007 she played six songs acoustically at True Music with Katie Daryl on Hdnet in Los Angeles, California, in an episode that aired on 2 September 2007.[124][125] The same month she performed on the Heaven and Earth Show aired on BBC One.[126] On 29 June 2007, O'Riordan took to the stage of Festivalbar in Catania, Italy.[127] On 2 August 2007, Sanctuary Records UK division ceased their activity and was acquired by UMG at about $88 million.[128] O'Riordan commented, "they started off as a management company for Iron Maiden, maybe 25 years ago. But they've been around forever and now they've become a record company, and I thought, that looks grand and solid—they're indie and they'll be good. Jesus, six months into Are you Listening? they got bought out by Universal in the States...".[129] On 19 November 2007, she cancelled the remainder of her European Tour (Lille, Paris, Luxembourg, Warsaw and Prague) due to illness.[130] In December 2007, she performed in a few small American clubs, including Des Moines, Nashville, and Charlottesville, Virginia.[131]

O'Riordan promoting her debut solo album Are You Listening? in 2007

In 2008, O'Riordan won an EBBA Award. Every year the European Border Breakers Awards recognize the success of ten emerging artists or groups who reached audiences outside their own countries with their first internationally released album in the past year.[132]

In January 2009, the University Philosophical Society (Trinity College, Dublin) invited the Cranberries to reunite for a concert celebrating O'Riordan's appointment as an honorary member of the Society, which led the band members to consider reuniting for a tour and a recording session.[133][134][135] Of the event, embracing her performance with the Cranberries, O'Riordan stated that "the minute we started playing it felt like we'd never stopped", pointing out that "it's a chemistry. It just fits".[136] O'Riordan released her second album No Baggage, featuring 11 tracks, in August 2009.[137] The first single "The Journey" was released on 13 July 2009, followed by a second single, "Switch Off the Moment". The music video for "The Journey" was directed by Robin Schmidt and filmed in 16 mm on 8 May 2009, at Howth Beach Pier and at Howth Summit, Dublin, Ireland. The music video aired on 29 July 2009.[138][139] O'Riordan said of No Baggage "I probably haven't worn my heart on my sleeve like this since the second album No Need to Argue".[137] Nevertheless, No Baggage was poorly received by music critics compared to Are you Listening?, and neither album replicated the success of the Cranberries.[140][141]

2009–2012: Comeback and Rosesedit
Main article: The Cranberries
O'Riordan performing with her signature Gibson SG electric guitar in Paris in May 2010[142]

On 25 August 2009, while promoting her solo album No Baggage in New York City on 101.9 RXP radio,[143] O'Riordan announced the Cranberries Reunion World Tour of 107 concerts.[134][144][145] O'Riordan reported that she had thought about how much she missed the band before making the decision to tour again. She added that Lawler and the two Hogan brothers were "a big part of my heart and soul".[146] O'Riordan and the Cranberries allowed their songs "Dreams", "Empty" along with "Apple Of My Eye" and "Stupid", to feature in the film[which?] released in the US in October 2013.[147][148][149]

The Cranberries reformed and the tour began in North America in mid-November, followed by South America in mid-January 2010 and Europe in March 2010.[144][145] The band played songs from O'Riordan's solo albums, many of The Cranberries' classics, as well as new songs.[150] In 2010, O'Riordan told Billboard magazine that playing with Fergal Lawler, Noel, and Mike Hogan worked better dynamically with her voice.[151] By 2010, O'Riordan suffered from vocal cord nodules which caused her doctor to prescribe six weeks of rest from performing. Consequently, concert dates were cancelled and postponed, but the recurring problem persisted until 2012.[152][153][154]

On 1 July 2011, a concert entitled "TU Warszawa"—"Here, Warsaw" was the main event of the inauguration of Poland's presidency of the EU council. O'Riordan performed "Zombie" and "I Lied" (English version of the Polish song "Skłamałam") with the Sinfonia Varsovia Orchestra, in Warsaw, Poland.[155][156] At this point in her career, to keep up with her bookings, negotiations and finances, O'Riordan began to be managed by Danny Goldberg, former Kurt Cobain and Nirvana manager. Goldberg has also managed Sonic Youth and Courtney Love's band Hole.[157][158][159] O'Riordan celebrated the reunion by touring with the Cranberries across Asia in July 2011, where the crowd was "impressed with her wide vocal range and strong vocal control".[160][161] During the six years of their hiatus, O'Riordan and Noel Hogan occasionally shared ideas.[162] In 2011, they recorded their sixth album, Roses with longtime producer Stephen Street, released in February 2012.[159]

O'Riordan in May 2012

On 22 March 2012, the Cranberries cancelled nine minutes before the show at the Enmore Theatre in Sydney, O'Riordan suffered from food poisoning and was unable to perform. When she recovered, the Roses Tour resumed two days later and the cancelled show was rescheduled for 26 March.[163] In May 2012, the final two concerts of the North American tour of the Cranberries had to be postponed for a then undisclosed reason, which was later said to involve from O'Riordan's "hectic touring schedule"; this caused some uncertainty about the upcoming European leg of the tour.[164] For the second leg of the Roses World Tour, O'Riordan hired a touring backing vocalist, Johanna Cranitch. During anterior tours, backup vocals were performed by the band's backup guitarist, Steve DeMarchi.[165][166] In November 2012, the extent to which her father's 2011 death was affecting O'Riordan was made public when she admitted in Le Télégramme that she was unable to perform "Ode to My Family" throughout the 32 shows of the second leg of the European tour; O'Riordan said "I hope to be able to sing it back one day, but for now, it's too soon".[167]

2013–2018: The Voice of Ireland and Something Elseedit
Main article: The Cranberries

O'Riordan replaced Sharon Corr as one of the mentors on RTÉ's The Voice of Ireland during the 2013–14 season.[168][169] O'Riordan reached the final of the competition with her act Kellie Lewis, who finished in second place.[170][171] In October 2013, O'Riordan and Marco Mendoza reconvened their partnership and were working on the songs for her announced third solo album scheduled for 2014, and presumably some film possibilities.[172] Her final performance at the Vatican Christmas concert occurred in December 2013,[78] where she performed "Letting Go" from Are You Listening?, "Silent Night" in duet with Elisa Toffoli, "Away in a Manger" and "Happy Xmas (War Is Over)".[79][173] In the autumn of 2013, as her hometown of Limerick was preparing to start its tenure as Irish City of Culture in 2014, O'Riordan was approached by the city to play a special gig.[174] During a New Year's Eve party under the Spire of St Mary's Cathedral, she performed with a quartet from the Irish Chamber Orchestra, playing "Linger", "Zombie" and one solo, "The Journey".[175]

In mid-January 2014, between shoots for The Voice, O'Riordan stated that she had written 15 songs for a solo album and she planned to go to Los Angeles to elaborate the start of the album.[176] In April 2014, disillusioned by her experiences in the music industry, O'Riordan told Barry Egan that the record business made her "extraordinarily wealthy, but sucked the blood out of her, like a particularly ferocious vampire".[177] In mid-July 2014, O'Riordan had announced that she would not return to The Voice of Ireland for a second season due to her health condition affected by flights from Dublin to Canada during seven weeks of filming.[171]

In April 2014, O'Riordan began recording new material with Jetlag, a collaboration with Andy Rourke of the Smiths and Olé Koretsky, a DJ and producer based in New York. They then formed a trio under the name D.A.R.K. Their first album, Science Agrees, was released in September 2016.[178][179]

In late April 2017, celebrating the 25th anniversary of the band, the Cranberries released a new studio album Something Else, featuring acoustic versions of their greatest hits, and backed by the Irish Chamber Orchestra. Three new songs appear on this album: "Rupture," "Why" and "The Glory" the last song written by O'Riordan and Noel Hogan, in their song-writing partnership.[180][181] The album was well received by critics; reviewers praised "the return of one of Ireland's finest songsmiths", and reacted favourably to the orchestral and acoustic reimagining.[181][182][183] Music critic Karen Gwee described O'Riordan's voice as "more measured, more labile and rich with maturity", whilst saying that "the thinness of her voice dilutes the anxious energy of "Animal Instinct", one of the album's tracks".[184]

In May 2017, the band started the world tour with acoustic concerts, with a string quartet. Most of the time, O'Riordan sang seated on a stool. After eleven shows, O'Riordan was said to be in "excruciating pain". The Cranberries published on social media the cancellation of the sold-out tour in Europe and North America, stating that O'Riordan's back problem was in the mid- to upper area of her spine and diaphragmatic movements associated with breathing and singing exacerbated the pain.[185][186] During her rest, O'Riordan had been planning a new album of the Cranberries, and had written and recorded demo versions in her final years.[187]

O'Riordan's last public performance was on 14 December 2017 in New York City, where she sang three Cranberries songs at Billboard's Christmas party.[188][189][190] On 15 December 2017, Eminem released his album Revival which included a large sample from the song "Zombie" as the hook for his rap song "In Your Head".[191]

Artistryedit
Influencesedit

O'Riordan's deeply religious mother had a strong influence on her musical development, introducing her to Elvis Presley at an early age.[192][193] O'Riordan's Catholic education and experience playing the church organ also introduced her to classical church music genres such as Gregorian chant, which she described as having "great melodies."[194][17][c][193][196] Months before she died, O'Riordan tested the resonance and the acoustics of the Glenstal Abbey church in Ireland to sing there.[197] O'Riordan stated that this apprenticeship by this detachment of the world in a raw and devoted setting influenced a lot of her development as an artist and as a musician.[65][149]

She referred to Presley and John Lennon as particularly large influences during her early years. Other early influences include Frank Sinatra, Jim Reeves and Bing Crosby.[198] In her teenage years, O'Riordan spent much of her time with her brothers who listened to heavy metal music,[8][199] while being equally passionate about rock and Gaelic folk music.[8][200]

When she had reached the age of 16,[17] O'Riordan had started listening to the Smiths,[96] the Cure,[96][201] R.E.M.,[92][202] and Depeche Mode,[92][203] which constituted her primary musical influences.[17] She had also been influenced by the Kinks,[204] Magazine,[205][206] Siouxsie and the Banshees,[202] and New Order.[24][205]

She credited Johnny McEvoy's song "The Old Bog Road" as one of the most beautiful old Irish songs and praised the Pogues' songs.[192] She made a reference to Ireland's most famous poet, William Butler Yeats.[207] O'Riordan stated of the grunge decade; "creatively it was a really great time", mentioning Pearl Jam, Blind Melon and Nirvana.[208] She wrote the song "I'm Still Remembering" six months after the death of Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain.[209][210] In 2009, talking about her three favourite albums, O'Riordan mentioned the Smiths' album The Smiths, Depeche Mode's album Violator, and the original soundtrack of the film The Mission.[211] Her other musical influences include Morrissey, Led Zeppelin,[212] also Metallica, and James Hetfield whom she met in 1995.[213][214][215] She drew her influences from everyday life, events that occurred in the world, or her friendly and romantic relationships.[216] Her yodeling signature came from listening to her father singing that way: she also cited female rock singers "like Sinéad O'Connor and Siouxsie Sioux".[217] O'Riordan realized that "it was something that could work into The Cranberries' format because a lot of that was used in religious Irish music".[217]

Songwriting and musicianshipedit

Take any artistry and you'll find a melancholic strain in the works of the best pioneers, an undying obsession with death, and a primal need to capture the wondrous, the bizarre each time.

— Writer Sneha Bengani's reaction to O'Riordan's death[218]

O'Riordan penned her first song, called "Calling", at the age of 12.[18][45][219] She was the lead lyricist and co-composer of the band's songs with guitarist Noel Hogan, although she wrote a lot of the song structures.[195][220] In the early days of the Cranberries, Hogan gave her a sequence of chords he had composed; a week later she came back with the completed lyrics of "Linger"[d] and wrote "Sunday" shortly after.[221][222] O'Riordan described in 1993 that she chose to be a singer and songwriter for the creative aspect, "something new", saying that she would not have been happy singing traditional Irish music for a living.[223] O'Riordan had a preference for solitude as an approach to writing songs. According to Hogan, the Cranberries never changed their writing process after their first encounter. Throughout their partnership, O'Riordan and Hogan never sat in a room together and wrote at the same time.[224]

O'Riordan performing in Montreal in 2009[225]

O'Riordan tended to write her ideas continuously through the day, although most of the melodies came in the night since she struggled with insomnia;[226] and so, she had a history of sleeping pills dependence in the course of her career.[227] She experienced writer's block for months during one period of her life.[226]

I draw from a lot of different life experiences: births, deaths, war, pain, depression, anger, sadness. [ ... ] I found it very easy to write lyrics when I was younger because I had no inhibitions—they just came pouring out. I find as I get older it's more difficult: you develop fears and you go, 'What will people think of this?' But it's important not to think too much about what people will think, because then you'll never write!

— Dolores O'Riordan, speaking of song themes in How I Wrote...: Songwriting Magazine.[228]

O'Riordan noted in Ultimate Guitar on her writing process, "lyrics are very important for me to make sure that I'm portraying whatever it is I need to portray. So I sit there but the funny thing is they've come to me anywhere". [ ... ] 'Oh, I have to go get a pen quick'. In the middle of the night when you're trying to go to sleep and they're going around in your head, your words, and you just get up and go out and write them down".[153] O'Riordan was easily bored and could not rest for a week,[229] Hogan described O'Riordan's routine working on her songs late at night or overnight: "her emails were like text messages. Fifteen of them, but they're all, like, two lines, at two o'clock in the morning."[230] O'Riordan wrote songs about themes that evolved over the course of her career, her experience taught her to never feel inhibited and always make an effort to try other things artistically.[231][232] O'Riordan stated in The Independent that she wrote about what is getting to her at the time, she said that writing lyrics was "about the things you need to talk about, I write to get my emotions out. It's self-therapeutic".[233]

In the National Post, music producer Dan Brodbeck commented that on the first day at the studio after being hired, she played him a few chords and a piano medley, then left him alone with little guidance.[234] O'Riordan came back a few hours later and accredited his work, then she took a microphone and started singing lyrics off the top of her head; Brodbeck stated: "it was always spur-of-the-moment, gut reaction stuff".[234] Gil Moore, owner of Metalworks Studios, referred to O'Riordan as "a God-given talent". Moore later stated, "she was the quintessential signature style artist, a very free spirit. She was the antithesis of a formula writer. She just went her own way".[235]

Voiceedit
"Pathetic Senses"
O'Riordan displayed one of her vocal capabilities on the Cranberries' trademark sound. The song captures O'Riordan soaring up to Soprano High C (C 6).[97]
Problems playing this file? See media help.

O'Riordan was a mezzo-soprano, with a vocal range from B 2 to C 6.[7][97][236] She did not sing much in the 5th octave but rather in a range of vocal comfort.[237] She was familiar with the vocal belting of '90s alternative rock[97] and was also devoted to her love of falsetto.[97][238][239] Her voice was rather light without applying an uncomfortable weight, and she characteristically deployed a soft projection when she sang the lowest notes.[97][240] O'Riordan's signature singing style integrated many elements, such as the lilting voice,[7][241] mournful keening,[242] glottal ornamentation and a distinctive attack on syllables.[180] Mikael Wood of Los Angeles Times commented, "She had a high, airy tone that could turn ferocious without warning. She emphasized its breaks and curls, decorating the catchy melodies she wrote with florid vocal runs inherited from Celtic tradition."[243] O'Riordan was also renowned for her yodeling techniques, embracing the sharp break of her voice.[244][245][246] She had never compromised her strong Irish accent, even when she was criticized for that.[245][247][248] Her singing was rooted in the Sean-nós vocal style;[244] the University of Limerick wrote, "Dolores's voice carried strong traces of the Sean-nós (old style) Gaelic tradition of unaccompanied singing that so beautifully conveys sadness, regret and loneliness."[249] "Íosa", an outtake from the Cranberries' debut album, was the only song in which O'Riordan sang entirely in Irish-Gaelic, inspired by her path as a liturgical soloist.[250] Around the age of 40, the timbre of her voice changed and became more mature.[e][153]

Melody Maker described O'Riordan's voice as "the voice of a saint trapped in a glass harp".[201][230] In a Billboard article, Dan Weiss remarked that her voice was "at her best, one of the most impressive".[61] Ireland's Prime Minister Leo Varadkar said O'Riordan was "the voice of a generation".[253][254] Weiss praised O'Riordan's vocal ability, commenting: "She knew she could multiply her phrases in harmony and clever aural sculpting, which turned relatively simple and round chord progressions like "Ode to My Family" into complex waterfalls of vocalization, and yet the jangling folk guitars buffering them were clearly armored by capital-R rock".[255]

Vocal recordingsedit
O'Riordan performing in 2010

Noel Hogan described how O'Riordan tended to "layer a lot of harmonies, a lot of falsetto stuff" as soon as she first entered the recording studio, Xeric Studios, at the beginning of 1990.[256] O'Riordan used a Neumann U 87 microphone for her vocal tracks, especially during the recording of the debut studio album Everybody Else Is Doing It, So Why Can't We?.[256] In an interview with Sound on Sound, in March 2019, Hogan and record producer Stephen Street said that "spontaneity was the key";[f] Hogan said: "she would like to do maybe three or four takes".[256] Regarding backing vocals she would go through very quickly, he said: "cause she had an amazing ear for tuning", then she ended with her highest notes.[256] She would add additional layers of vocal inflections over the existing main vocals as she went along.[256] In the South China Morning Post, Hogan described O'Riordan's voice during the recording of "Linger": We're all looking at each in the room going, 'where did that come out from?' because she was so small and tiny—you didn't expect that. And then she only grew from that point on. As the years went down, she just got better and better."[257]

O'Riordan was recognized for her raw natural voice,[258][259] Hogan corroborated this on Officialcharts, he stated: "we weren't going to start using Auto-Tune and all that shite. She would absolutely kill us",[260] speaking of the production of the band's latest album, In the End, created from demo vocals recorded by O'Riordan before her death.[260] O'Riordan tended to let her breathing be heard on the albums, preferring to focus on the delivery while emphasizing expressiveness and nuance rather than being perfectionist, saying "keep it natural, keep it real"—adding, "when it's too clean, when people go in and try to clean up the breath to make it sound seamless, it takes away from the reality".[17] The voice recording protocol had evolved over the years, O'Riordan was worried about "oversinging and smothering the raw emotion in her delivery", as a result, she did not come to work in studios during daylight hours with Fergal Lawler and the two Hogan brothers.[229][230] Lawler told David Browne in a 2019 Rolling Stone interview: "Dolores would come in to do the vocals and we'd have a chat. She'd have a listen to what we'd done and then we'd head off and let her do her thing. So in the evening time, you're almost looking out in the corridor to see if she's coming in."[229]

Personal lifeedit

On 18 July 1994, O'Riordan married Canadian-born Don Burton, who was the former tour manager of Duran Duran.[20][261] They met in the U.S. while Duran Duran and the Cranberries were on tour together.[16][29] The wedding was held at Holy Cross Abbey in County Tipperary.[29][77] The couple had three children.[261][262] O'Riordan had a stepson from Burton's previous relationship.[261][262] In 1996, they lived at The Coach House, a medieval-style residence beside Ballyhannon Castle at Quin in County Clare, Ireland.[263] They lived in their first home for a year while they planned their own ultra-modern house,[263] including a recording studio and guest apartment, set on a 16-acre (6.5-hectare) plot in Dunquin, west County Kerry, on the Dingle Peninsula, but they spent little time there and later sold the property.[264][265]

In 1998, the couple bought a 150-acre (61-hectare) stud farm, called Riversfield Stud, located in Kilmallock, County Limerick, before selling it for US$5 million in 2004.[264] They then moved to Howth, County Dublin, where O'Riordan acquired a house in 2004; she later sold the house in 2010.[266] The family spent summers in a log cabin on a property they bought in 1994 near Buckhorn, Ontario, Canada.[citation needed][267]

Former mansion of O'Riordan and Don Burton, large house to the far right, on the tip of the Dingle Peninsula in Ireland. The mansion dominated a hillside in Dún Chaoin and was nicknamed "Dolly's Folly" by some locals due to its construction of massive proportions into the landscape.[268]

Raised as a Roman Catholic, O'Riordan was an admirer of Pope John Paul II,[269] whom she met in 2001 and 2002.[77][270] She was also interested in hurling and played the sport as a child.[271][272] In 2018, Limerick bridged a 45-year gap to win the 2018 All-Ireland SHC, and "Dreams" by The Cranberries was played at Croke Park to coincide with the festivities.[273] The team later brought the trophy to her family home.[274][272]

In 2009, O'Riordan and her family moved full-time to Buckhorn, Ontario, living in a waterfront home on Big Bald Lake.[267]

In October 2009, O'Riordan attended an event at The Westwood Theatre in Ontario, after a screening of South Dakota: A Woman's Right to Choose, a film about teenage pregnancy and abortion.[147] O'Riordan moderated a discussion with high school pupils; she remained neutral and allowed the girls to formulate their own opinions.[275]

On 25 November 2011, O'Riordan's father died at his home in Limerick after six years of fighting cancer. According to O'Riordan, he held on to celebrate his 50th wedding anniversary on 14 November.[9]

In July 2013, O'Riordan and her family moved to the exclusive area of Abington, in the north of Dublin, and they eventually developed the idea of buying a house.[168][276]

In October 2013, O'Riordan told journalist and close friend Barry Egan in the Sunday Independent's Life magazine that she had attempted suicide by overdosing on medication, but "wanted to live for her kids".[177] O'Riordan also spoke publicly of her painful personal history.[277][278] O'Riordan was sexually abused by a family friend for four years from the ages of 8 to 12.[251][279] She developed depression, deep self-loathing and suicidal thoughts over the years which were worsened by her accelerating career and led to anorexia.[251][279] Afterward, she said that she continued to move forward for her children and her husband.[280] At her father's funeral in 2011, O'Riordan's abuser introduced himself to her and apologized for his actions.[251][279] O'Riordan said in 2013 "I had nightmares for a year before my father's death about meeting him. ... I didn't see him for years and years and then I saw him at my father's funeral. I had blocked him out of my life".[251][278][279]

O'Riordan's family moved back to Canada in November 2013, considering they were used to the outdoors and the wilderness.[276] Towards the end of 2013, O'Riordan returned to live in Ireland; this decision preceded the end of her marriage.[261][267]

O'Riordan and her husband Burton ended their marriage in September 2014 after 20 years together.[281][282] Following her split from Burton, O'Riordan suffered from serious depression in 2014 and her mental health issues were compounded by alcohol use.[283] O'Riordan left Canada and moved to New York City, living first in a hotel in Union Square and then at Trump Tower.[281]

On 10 November 2014, O'Riordan was arrested and charged in connection with air rage on an Aer Lingus flight from JFK International Airport to Shannon Airport.[251] During the flight, she became verbally and physically abusive to the crew. When police were arresting her, she resisted, reminding them that her taxes paid their wages and shouting, "I'm the Queen of Limerick! I'm an icon!", headbutting one Garda officer and spitting at another.[284] She allegedly fractured the air hostess's foot during the incident and was medically assessed at University Hospital, escorted by Shannon Police.[285] Following her arrest, O'Riordan spent three weeks in a psychiatric hospital. She later pleaded guilty to the charges.[286] Eileen O'Riordan stated that her daughter was in a fragile mental state and that medical results indicated there was no alcohol or drugs detected in her daughter's system.[287] The judge hearing her case agreed to dismiss all charges if she apologized in writing to her victims and contributed €6,000 ($7,300) to the court poor box.[284] Later, O'Riordan told the media that she had been stressed from living in New York hotels following the end of her 20-year marriage.[281] Her family described Dolores as "strong-minded and determined";[288] however, discussing her mental instability and her volatile vulnerability in a 2014 interview with the Belfast Telegraph, O'Riordan explained that she "carried quite a burden of pain and torment from (her) past".[251][283]

In January 2015, O'Riordan returned to the U.S., where she bought an apartment in the East Village of New York.[289] Also in 2015, O'Riordan developed a relationship with the U.S. musician Olé Koretsky, with whom she shared the last years of her life.[290] In 2017, O'Riordan bought a new house near her hometown of Limerick.[291]

In May 2017, O'Riordan publicly discussed her bipolar disorder, stating that she had been diagnosed in 2015.[292] According to one writer, music was more a therapy than a commodity for O'Riordan.[91] O'Riordan admitted that "there have been times when I've struggled. The death of my father and mother-in-law was very hard. Looking back, I think depression, whatever the cause, is one of the worst things to go through. Then again, I've also had a lot of joy in my life, especially with my children. You get ups as well as downs. Sure, isn't that what life's all about?"[91]

O'Riordan started writing a suicide note in September 2017 during a period of taking lorazepam and drinking.[293] An American psychotherapist assessed O'Riordan on 26 December 2017, suggesting an abstinence from alcohol and noting no suicidal thoughts.[293]

O'Riordan's final social media post, looking to the future, occurred on 4 January 2018.[190]

Wealthedit

In 2006, she was one of the 10 richest women in Ireland,[294] and was reported to be the fifth-richest woman in 1999.[201][295] In 2008, she was sixth on the list of the ten richest artists in Ireland; her net worth was $66 million.[296]

Deathedit

On 15 January 2018, O'Riordan was found unresponsive in the bathroom of a London hotel room and pronounced dead at 9:16 a.m. She was 46.[297][298] An inquest at Westminster Coroner's Court held on 6 September,[299][300] ruled that she died as a result of accidental drowning in a bath following sedation by alcohol intoxication.[299][301] Empty bottles were found in O'Riordan's room (five miniature bottles and a champagne bottle) as well as some prescription drugs. Toxicology tests showed that her body contained only "therapeutic" levels of these medications but had a blood alcohol content of 330 mg/dL (0.33%).[299][301]

O'Riordan was living in New York City at the time of her death. She had travelled to London to work with Martin "Youth" Glover on her side-project D.A.R.K. and to meet representatives of the BMG record label about a new Cranberries album.[302][303][304] O'Riordan arrived at the Hilton Hotel on Park Lane, Mayfair, on 14 January.[297] At 2 a.m. on the morning of her death, O'Riordan had a phone call with her mother.[305]

The day after O'Riordan's death, the tabloid newspaper Santa Monica Observer spread a false story stating that fentanyl had been found in her room and that London authorities suspected that she had committed suicide.[306] The fentanyl overdose rumour endured for months.[307]

O'Riordan's grave (pictured in 2018)
O'Riordan's and her father's tombstone at Caherelly Cemetery in Herbertstown
Memorial serviceedit

A three-day funeral in her hometown, with O'Riordan lying in repose, lasted from 20 to 22 January at St Joseph's Church. In a tribute normally reserved for heads of state, thousands streamed past her open coffin in a four-hour public reposing inside the church.[308][309] O'Riordan, wearing dark eyeshadow, with raven hair, was laid out wearing black and holding a set of pearl rosary beads.[309][310] O'Riordan's music was played, while photographs of the singer performing one of her songs and posing with Pope John Paul II were placed along the walls.[304][311] Friends left a floral tribute next to the coffin, which read: "The song has ended, but the memories linger on".[311][312] Young and old travelled from all over the world—including from Spain, China and South America—to pay their respects in person.[309][313]

O'Riordan was buried on 23 January after a service at Saint Ailbe's Roman Catholic Church, Ballybricken, County Limerick;[304][311] it began with the studio recording of "Ave Maria" as sung by O'Riordan and Luciano Pavarotti.[314][315] At the end of the service, the Cranberries' song "When You're Gone" was played.[316][317] Among the attendees at her funeral were her mother, Eileen; her three children and their father, O'Riordan's former husband, Don Burton; her sister and brothers; all Cranberries members; O'Riordan's boyfriend, Olé Koretsky; Ireland's president, Michael D. Higgins; former rugby union player Ronan O'Gara; and Bono's wife, Ali Hewson.[304][314][315] O'Riordan was buried alongside her father.[304][317]

Remembrancesedit
Recognitionedit

The President of Ireland at the time, Michael D. Higgins, was one of the first to pay his respects.[318] The Taoiseach of Ireland, Leo Varadkar, also paid his respects to O'Riordan.[319] Also, in recognition of O'Riordan's influence, the Avett Brothers covered the Cranberries song "Linger".[320] Bono and Johnny Depp performed a tribute for O'Riordan ending the performance on "Linger", at the National Concert Hall in Dublin, Ireland, just hours after the sudden death of O'Riordan.[321] Bono, Sinéad O'Connor, Johnny Depp and Nick Cave gave Dolores O'Riordan a standing ovation at a birthday party for Shane MacGowan, singer of the Pogues.[321] On the announcement of her death on 15 January 2018, O'Riordan appeared on the huge 360° screen overhanging the Madison Square Garden floor in New York City during a New York Rangers game. A photo of this appearance was published on 17 January 2018 on Madison Square Garden's Facebook.[322]

Among those honouring O'Riordan were the Cranberries,[323] Olé Koretsky,[324] Andy Rourke (former bassist of the Smiths),[324] Stephen Street,[325] U2,[326] Duran Duran,[327] Julian Lennon,[328] Liz Phair,[329] James Corden,[327] Josh Groban,[327] Roger Bennett,[330] Hozier,[327] Foster the People,[327] Elijah Wood,[323] Peter Cornell (brother of Chris Cornell, who died May of the previous year),[331] Mark Lanegan,[327] Pearl Jam,[332] Bryan Adams,[323] Halsey,[333] Kodaline,[327] the The,[323] Michael Stipe and R.E.M.,[333] Dave Davies of the Kinks,[329] Adele,[326] Garbage,[332] Annie Lennox,[334] Cerys Matthews,[326] Lisa Stansfield,[326] Michelle Branch,[329] Dan Brodbeck,[335] Slash,[328] Graham Hopkins,[330] Benjamin Kowalewicz,[330] Vic Fuentes,[323] actors Luke Evans[323] and Francois Arnaud,[329] Questlove,[336] Kiesza,[327] Diplo,[327] Gao Xiaosong,[337] Colin Parry,[323] The Tim Parry Johnathan Ball Foundation for Peace,[338] Ali Hewson,[82] Adi Roche[82] and Chernobyl Children International.[82] On 29 March 2018, Mayor Stephen Keary presented the book of condolences with over 16,000 signatures to O'Riordan's mother Eileen, brothers Donal, Terry and Joe, and other family members.[339]

Further reactionedit

The Kinks guitarist Dave Davies, a close friend of O'Riordan, had planned to collaborate on songs together before she died; they had an idea for a song called "Home"—"about being home again".[204]

Just prior to her death on 15 January 2018, while she was in London for a studio mixing session with Youth on D.A.R.K.'s second album, O'Riordan left a voice message—the last one she would ever leave—at 1:12 a.m. to her longtime friend, Dan Waite, who coordinated a recording session of a "Zombie" cover that he had previously given O'Riordan to listen to and accredit.[340] According to Waite, she offered "to sing on it" on Christmas Eve 2017.[341][342] TMZ published this voice message on 5 April 2018.[340] On 18 January 2018, the heavy metal band Bad Wolves released this cover of "Zombie", which charted on multiple Billboard charts.[343][344]

On 28 January 2018, the In Memoriam segment of the 60th Annual Grammy Awards honored a number of music icons, including O'Riordan.[345]

"Dreams" was played in Croke Park to the 82,000-capacity crowd on 19 August 2018, after Limerick GAA won the Liam MacCarthy Cup in the All-Ireland Senior Hurling Championship for the first time in 45 years.[346] The cup was later toured around Limerick and was brought by the team to O'Riordan's family home in Ballybricken.[272]

On 24 April 2019, Saint Sister, a duo from Northern Ireland, performed an a cappella rendition of "Dreams" at the funeral in St Anne's Cathedral in Belfast[347] of Lyra McKee; McKee, some allege, was killed by the New IRA on 18 April 2019.[348]

Aftermathedit

In mid-September 2018, bandmate Noel Hogan confirmed that the Cranberries would disband after releasing their final album, In the End.[349][350] He said: "We don't want to continue without Dolores, so we're just going to leave after this".[349][351]

On 6 September 2023 (which would have been O'Riordan's 52nd birthday), the upcoming release of an album of solo songs that O'Riordan had recorded a few years before her death was announced.[352]

Posthumous salesedit

The Cranberries dominated Amazon's music digital sales in the 24 hours following O'Riordan's death announcement, with sales surging on the site by 913,350% of their album Something Else. O'Riordan's solo work Are You Listening? was ranked second. The Cranberries' albums also dominated Amazon's ranking of physical CD and vinyl sales, along with her solo album, No Baggage, seeing an increase in sales of 200,000%. Four albums of the Cranberries reached the iTunes Top 10 Albums chart, with Stars: The Best of 1992–2002 peaking at No. 2.[353][354] The band's biggest hits, including "Linger", "Dreams" and "Zombie", ranked in the top five most-downloaded digital songs on Amazon's list, and ranked in the top 10 of the iTunes songs chart.[354][355]

Legacyedit
O'Riordan's No Need to Argue–era outfit displayed at the Hard Rock Cafe, Chicago

O'Riordan has been referred to as "one of the most distinctive voices in alternative rock history".[61][250][356] Through her impact on the music industry, she has been described as "one of the most recognisable voices in pop culture".[357] O'Riordan also brought an "inimitable" and "unique voice" to the 1990s' music scene and to rock music.[7][358][359] She is considered an "icon of Irish pop"[360] and a "1990s rock icon".[358][361][362][363]

Recording Academy contributor Philip Merrill called O'Riordan "a gifted songwriter and vocalist whose ballads helped define alt-pop in the 1990s".[364] She was credited for her innovative style embodied by her "measured vocal power, her honest, vulnerable songwriting", reinforced by her Irish accent, thus helping the Cranberries to rise "into worldwide stardom".[365] Music industry publication Billboard considered the song "Linger" as "pure Irish poetry", while "Dreams", which contains no chorus, is regarded as "one of the greatest songs of all time".[5][366] Amanda Petrusich wrote how she deviated from the norm, saying that most of the other rock singers at the time sounded "plainly and hopelessly cool—disaffected, vaguely antagonistic and aloof", while "O'Riordan sounded like a maniac".[367] Following news of O'Riordan's death, U2 described O'Riordan's music, and vocal style with these words: "out of the West came this storm of a voice—she had such strength of conviction, yet she could speak to the fragility in all of us".[368] Hozier and Foster the People called O'Riordan "a true pioneer" for future generations.[327][368]

According to Hot Press' Stuart Clark, who wrote the press release for the Cranberries' first cassette EP, O'Riordan was an artist who "left an indelible mark". He also referred to her as an Irish female icon.[369][370] TV producer Larry Bass regarded her as "not only an icon but an Irish female icon. Very few Irish women had achieved the heights that she had on a global stage".[169] For contemporary Ireland's singers, O'Riordan is considered a "beacon for future generations of singers", stated Hot Press editorial writer Peter McGoran.[371] Irish President Michael D Higgins praised O'Riordan's and the band's "immense influence on rock and pop music in Ireland and internationally".[336]

A place of pilgrimage, the grave of O'Riordan continues to attract devotees from around the world.[180][372] O'Riordan's commitment to her roots, which was consolidated by her authenticity, attracted fascination.[180] According to Una Mullally of The New York Times, O'Riordan's native accent positioned the Cranberries as a "truly" Irish band, which maintained its cultural identity and integrity, whose "global success was instigated by how America embraced them", by their music videos in "heavy rotation", and "crucially, by American radio".[62] Rolling Stone stated that in 1995 the Cranberries were "Ireland's biggest musical export since U2".[368] Paul Sexton of Billboard and the Australian Broadcasting Corporation have acknowledged O'Riordan and the Cranberries' influence on people, citing them as "one of the biggest-selling rock bands of the '90s".[224][373] Ethnomusicologist Dr. Aileen Dillane commented that "countless other writers and Twitter commentators reminisced upon how the band seemed to encapsulate the '90s zeitgeist and on the profound impact they and Dolores as lead singer had on their lives and sense of who (and where) they were in the world at that time".[180] In 2018, Hannah Tindle of Another Magazine wrote that "her strength of character shone through in the songs she wrote that remain, to this day, some of the most seminal in music history".[374]

In January 2018, the Dallas Observer listed O'Riordan alongside David Bowie, Prince and Tom Petty as iconic musicians who died between 2016 and 2018.[375] In 2018, the South Coast Herald stated that "Dolores O'Riordan and the Cranberries inspired millions".[376] O'Riordan inspired contemporary artists around the world while having a lasting impact on various musical styles;[377] following news of her death, Maggie Rogers said, "Dolores O'Riordan's voice helped me understand my place in the world."[378] AsiaOne argued that the Cranberries—especially O'Riordan's voice and singing style—have influenced many Chinese musicians and have had an unprecedented lasting impact on popular music across Asia.[160] The BBC added that O'Riordan was a major musical influence to Faye Wong, one of China's biggest pop stars.[337] Others influenced by O'Riordan include Florence Welch,[359] Adele,[359][379] Halsey,[333] Heather Baron-Gracie,[380] Michelle Branch[364] and Avril Lavigne.

O'Riordan was regarded as a humanitarian activist advocating for children throughout the world; most of the songs of O'Riordan communicated her empathy with human suffering and reflected popular hope for peace.[82][381][382] The Tim Parry Johnathan Ball Foundation for Peace stated that O'Riordan "left a legacy through her music that speaks for so many of us and called on all of us to follow a path of peace".[338]

On 19 February 2018, RTÉ One broadcast a 40-minute documentary about O'Riordan entitled Dolores. The documentary was produced by Dave Fanning and included never-before-seen interviews.[383]

Notesedit
 When Niall Quinn left the band, brothers Mike and Noel Hogan and Fergal Lawler remained without a singer for more than six months; during that time, they were an instrumental band working on demos.[44]
 It was not until 2010 that the countdown featured a female-fronted band in the No. 1 song, with Julia Stone and her brother Angus.[55] In 2019, Billie Eilish became the first solo woman to win Triple J Hottest 100.[57]
 O'Riordan said in 2001 "One of the most amazing experiences of my life was to go into a monastery and see monks coming out at 6am and start chanting. I used to go to monasteries to get away from the whole world and all the crap that comes from teenage pressures".[195]
 A song she wrote about being rejected. O'Riordan said "some years later, after I was married, the guy Linger is about wrote me a long letter, saying: 'I know the song's about me. I never meant to hurt your feelings. Can we meet?' I thought: It's too late. You dumped me!".[221]
 O'Riordan smoked cigarettes excessively under the influence of alcohol.[251] The extreme use of falsetto was also mentioned, although she managed to nuance with a "high, breathy voice".[252]
 O'Riordan was especially shy in the earliest vocal sessions for the Cranberries' 1993 debut album and did not want to stay in the control room without her boyfriend. Stephen Street managed to win her confidence after four or five songs into the album—"the magic happens then", recalled Street.[256]

[](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fivorsacademy.com%2Fnews%2Fwinners-of-the-ivors-2022-announced%2F&title=Winners+of+The+Ivors+2022+announced)[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fivorsacademy.com%2Fnews%2Fwinners-of-the-ivors-2022-announced%2F)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Winners+of+The+Ivors+2022+announced&url=https%3A%2F%2Fivorsacademy.com%2Fnews%2Fwinners-of-the-ivors-2022-announced%2F&via=Crunchify)

The Ivors Academy has announced this year's winners, celebrating the very best in songwriting and composing for screen.

![Image 4: Winners_GeneralGradientArtworks_WebNews2-scaled-1](https://ivorsacademy.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Winners_GeneralGradientArtworks_WebNews2-scaled-1-150x90.jpg)

The Ivors Academy has announced the winners of this year’s Ivor Novello Awards at Grosvenor House, London, on Thursday 19 th May.

Recognised as a pinnacle of creative musical achievement since they were first presented in 1956, winning an Ivor Novello Award holds a special place in music, as they are judged by award-winning songwriters and composers from The Ivors Academy.

In the 67 th year of The Ivors, 21 songwriters and composers collected Ivor Novello Awards across 14 categories, in recognition of outstanding achievements in songwriting and composing for screen.

This year’s **Songwriter of the Year** accolade has been awarded to rapper **Dave**. Having dropped the surprise Top 10 single _Titanium_ in 2021, Dave’s second album _We’re All Alone In This Together_ then hit number one in the UK. It spawned three simultaneous Top 10 singles – _Clash_, featuring Stormzy, _Verdansk_ and _In The Fire._

Dave’s 2021 wasn’t just restricted to his own superlative work however - as part of his ongoing collaboration with Fredo, he co-wrote the huge tracks, _Back To Basics_ and _Money Talks_. This is Dave’s fourth Ivor Novello Award, having previously won Best Contemporary Song three times for _Question Time_ in 2018, _Black_ in 2020 and _Children of the Internet_ last year.

With a catalogue of over 140 songs and more than 80 million record sales, the **Special International Award with Apple Music**celebrates the global impact and songwriting achievements of Columbian superstar **Shakira**.

**Ed Sheeran,****Fred again..** and**Johnny McDaid**, together win **PRS for Music Most Performed Work** for their collaboration on the UK’s biggest song of 2021, **_Bad Habits_**. This is Ed Sheeran’s fifth Ivor Novello Award, having won this category in 2018, along with Johnny McDaid for _Shape of You,_ Best Song Musically and Lyrically back in 2012 for _The A Team_ and Songwriter of the Year twice. It is songwriter and producer Fred again..’s first Ivor Novello Award.

Previous nominee **Sam Fender** has taken home his first Ivor Novello Award after winning **Best Song Musically and Lyrically,**for his hit **_Seventeen Going Under_**. The song chronicles Fender’s life at the age of 17 and the challenges he and his mother faced.

**Best Contemporary Song** went to **Dean ‘Inflo’ Josiah Cover**and **Little Simz** for **_I Love You, I Hate You_**. A searingly honest, poignant and powerful address to Little Simz’ father from the album _Sometimes I Might Be Introvert_. This win follows the pair’s success in 2020 when they collected an Ivor Novello Award for the album _Grey Area_.

The **Rising Star Award with Apple Music** has been awarded to singer-songwriter **Naomi Kimpenu**, whose debut EP _Prelude_ was released last year. The stunning four-track collection is described by The Ivors Academy as, _“the ideal calling card, serving notice of what her perfectly poised vocals and sincere songwriting can do.”_ She is the third consecutive female songwriter to pick up the award since its inception in 2020.

_Pink Noise_, performed and written by **Laura Mvula** with **Dann Hume**, wins **Best Album**. _Pink Noise_ is described as an album borne out of both intense struggles, positive realisations, and an exploration of personal and professional breakups.

**Daniel Blumberg** wins **Best Original Film Score** for his work on **_The World To Come_**_,_ seeing him receive his first Ivor Novello Award. Set against the backdrop of the mid-19th century American East Coast frontier, the film had its world premiere at the 77th Venice International Film Festival, where it won the Queer Lion award for best LGBTQI+ themed film at the festival, before it was released last year.

Composer **Arthur Sharpe** has won **Best Television Soundtrack** for his work on Sky Atlantic’s black comedy drama, **_Landscapers,_** based on a true-story and starring Emmy, Golden Globe and Academy Award winner Olivia Coleman.

The award for **Best Original Video Game Score** goes to **Richard Jacques** for **_Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy_**. Richard’s previous work includes critically acclaimed orchestral scores for blockbuster franchises such as _James Bond 007: Blood Stone,Sonic the Hedgehog_ and _Starship Troopers._

**Peter Gabriel**received **Fellowship of The Ivors Academy** in recognition of his outstanding contributions as a musician, innovator, humanitarian and songwriter. Fellowship is the highest honour the Academy bestows, recognising excellence and impact in the art and craft of music creation. Peter has previously won Ivor Novello Awards for _Don’t Give Up_ in 1987, for his Outstanding Contribution to British Music as a founding member of Genesis in 1983 and was recognised with a Lifetime Achievement award in 2007.

The **PRS for Music Icon Award** recognises two of rock’s most inspiring, influential, and identifiable songwriters – **The Cure’s Robert Smith** and **Simon Gallup**. They are true cultural icons who have changed the face of popular music across the last four decades as songwriters for The Cure.

**Paul Heaton** has been awarded **Outstanding Song Collection** for his work with **The Housemartins** through to **The Beautiful South**and his current collaboration with Jacqui Abbott. He has shown an exceptional talent at observing, and challenging society with a pop sensibility that has resulted in eighteen UK Top 10 albums and a place as one of this country’s finest songwriters.

In recognition of the influence of the unique sound world of Scottish band **Cocteau Twins**, The Ivors Academy also celebrated the creative genius of songwriters **Elizabeth Fraser**, **Robin Guthrie** and **Simon Raymonde** with the **Visionary Award**.

Also announced at the ceremony was the retirement of long-time ceremony host **Paul Gambaccini.** Paul hosted his first Ivor Novello Award ceremony in 1988 and has presented the awards every year since, only missing 2020 when the winners were announced online. In recognition of this, Academy Fellow Joan Armatrading presented him with a unique statuette to acknowledge his contribution to the awards. The Academy also announced that the new host for The Ivors in 2023 is **Lauren Laverne**.

At the ceremony last year’s Songwriter of the Year Jamie Hartman and multi award-winning producer and musician Paul Epworth gave their backing to [**TheWRD from The Ivors Academy**](https://studythewrd.com/), a recently launched pre-degree diploma in creative entrepreneurship. TheWRD is designed to help open access to the creative industries by bringing together music industry leaders, expert educators and deep learning AI to provide new opportunities for students aged 19 plus to start a career in the music industry or go onto further study.

**Shaznay Lewis, Ivor Novello Award winner and judge for The Ivors, said,**“_I’m absolutely thrilled for this year’s winners, who have joined an ever-expanding list of legendary songwriters and screen composers._ _It is a privilege to experience such an_ _immensely powerful, emotive and eclectic range of music_ _._ _Huge_ _congratulations to everyone who took home awards, and every single songwriter and composer nominated_.”

**Peter Brian Gabriel** (born 13 February 1950) is an English singer-songwriter, musician, and human rights activist. He is known for being a co-founder and the lead vocalist of [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)") for their first eight years and for his subsequent solo career. A winner of multiple major awards, he has been inducted into the [Rock and Roll Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_and_Roll_Hall_of_Fame "Rock and Roll Hall of Fame") as a member of Genesis and as a solo artist.

While attending [Charterhouse School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charterhouse_School "Charterhouse School") in Surrey, Gabriel co-founded Genesis in 1967. As the band's lead vocalist and principal lyricist, several of the albums released during his tenure, such as _[Nursery Cryme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nursery\_Cryme "Nursery Cryme")_ (1971), [_Foxtrot_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foxtrot_(album) "Foxtrot (album)") (1972) and _[Selling England by the Pound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selling\_England\_by\_the\_Pound "Selling England by the Pound")_ (1973), are considered [progressive rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Progressive_rock "Progressive rock") classics.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-hudak-1) Known for his theatrical performances and stage costumes, Gabriel's relations with his bandmates became strained around the release of the concept album _[The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Lamb\_Lies\_Down\_on\_Broadway "The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway")_ in 1974, and he left the band in 1975 following a world tour to support the album. Genesis continued with drummer [Phil Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Collins "Phil Collins") handling lead vocals. Gabriel took a brief musical hiatus before launching a successful solo career with four self-titled studio albums, which spanned progressive rock, [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"), [post-punk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-punk "Post-punk"), and [world music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music") styles. They contained the hit singles "[Solsbury Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solsbury_Hill_(song) "Solsbury Hill (song)")" (1977), "[Games Without Frontiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Games_Without_Frontiers_(song) "Games Without Frontiers (song)")" (1980), "[Shock the Monkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shock_the_Monkey "Shock the Monkey")" (1982), and "[Biko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biko_(song) "Biko (song)")" (1980), a protest song against [apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") in South Africa.

In 1986, Gabriel released the [worldbeat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worldbeat "Worldbeat")-influenced album _[So](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/So\_(album) "So (album)")_, his best-selling release; it is certified triple-platinum in the UK and quintuple-platinum in the US. Considered to be one of the [best albums of the 1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_1980s_albums_considered_the_best "List of 1980s albums considered the best"), it transformed him from a cult artist into an international superstar. The album's most successful single, "[Sledgehammer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sledgehammer_(Peter_Gabriel_song) "Sledgehammer (Peter Gabriel song)")", won a record nine [MTV Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV_Video_Music_Awards "MTV Video Music Awards") at the [1987 MTV Video Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_MTV_Video_Music_Awards "1987 MTV Video Music Awards"). A 2011 _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ report said "Sledgehammer" was the most played music video of all time on [MTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MTV "MTV").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Time-2) He released further albums _[Us](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Us\_(Peter\_Gabriel\_album) "Us (Peter Gabriel album)")_ (1992) and _[Up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Up\_(Peter\_Gabriel\_album) "Up (Peter Gabriel album)")_ (2002), the latter his last album of new songs for 21 years. During the interim, he contributed the song "[Down to Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_to_Earth_(Peter_Gabriel_song) "Down to Earth (Peter Gabriel song)")" to the [Pixar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pixar "Pixar") film _[WALL-E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WALL-E "WALL-E")_ (2008), recorded a cover album of other artists' songs, _[Scratch My Back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scratch\_My\_Back "Scratch My Back")_ (2010), and sponsored a companion album on which his own songs were covered by the same artists, _[And I'll Scratch Yours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/And\_I'll\_Scratch\_Yours "And I'll Scratch Yours")_ (2013). He embarked on the [Back to Front Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_Front_Tour "Back to Front Tour") (2012–14), and the Rock Paper Scissors Tour with [Sting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sting_(musician) "Sting (musician)") (2016). Gabriel released a new album, _[I/O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I/O\_(album) "I/O (album)")_, in 2023, and supported it with the [I/O The Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I/O_The_Tour "I/O The Tour") that year. He has been releasing songs to the lunar cycle for the follow-up album _[O\I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/O%5CI "O\I")_ (2026).

A supporter of world music for much of his career, Gabriel co-founded the [World of Music, Arts and Dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_of_Music,_Arts_and_Dance "World of Music, Arts and Dance") (WOMAD) festival in 1982 and wrote the [soundtrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Passion_(Peter_Gabriel_album) "Passion (Peter Gabriel album)") for [Martin Scorsese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Scorsese "Martin Scorsese")'s film [_The Last Temptation of Christ_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Last_Temptation_of_Christ_(film) "The Last Temptation of Christ (film)") (1988), which is considered a landmark in the world and [new age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_age "New age") genres. He founded [Real World Studios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_World_Studios "Real World Studios") in Wiltshire, where he produces and promotes world music through his [Real World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_World_Records "Real World Records") label. Gabriel was an early pioneer of [digital distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_distribution "Digital distribution") methods for music through his co-founding of [OD2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OD2 "OD2"), one of the first online music download services.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-3) He has also been involved in numerous humanitarian efforts. Beginning with [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International")’s [A Conspiracy of Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Conspiracy_of_Hope "A Conspiracy of Hope") tour in 1986, he has headlined several human rights benefit concerts, including Amnesty's [Human Rights Now!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Rights_Now! "Human Rights Now!") tour in 1988, and co-created the human rights organisation [Witness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witness_(organization) "Witness (organization)") in 1992.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Lynskey_2007-4) He developed the idea for [The Elders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Elders_(organization) "The Elders (organization)"), an organisation of public figures recognised as peace activists, alongside [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela") and [Richard Branson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Branson "Richard Branson") in 2007.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-5)

Gabriel has won three [Brit Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brit_Awards "Brit Awards"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-6) seven [Grammy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammy_Awards "Grammy Awards"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-7) 13 MTV Video Music Awards,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] the inaugural Pioneer Award at the [BT Digital Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BT_Digital_Music_Awards "BT Digital Music Awards"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-8) the _[Q](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Q\_(magazine) "Q (magazine)")_ Lifetime Achievement,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-9) the Ivor Novello Award for Lifetime Achievement,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-10) and the [Polar Music Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polar_Music_Prize "Polar Music Prize").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-11) He was named a [BMI Icon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broadcast_Music,_Inc. "Broadcast Music, Inc.") at the 57th annual BMI London Awards for his "influence on generations of music makers".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-12) In recognition of his human rights activism, he received the [Man of Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Man_of_Peace "Man of Peace") award from the [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize") laureates in 2006,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-13) and _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ magazine named him one of the 100 most influential people worldwide in 2008.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-14)[AllMusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllMusic "AllMusic") has described him as "one of rock's most ambitious, innovative musicians, as well as one of its most political".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Peter_Gabriel_AllMusic-15) In 2026, _[Loudwire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loudwire "Loudwire")_ ranked him as the second greatest progressive rock singer of all time.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-loudgreat-16) In recognition of his musical achievements, he was awarded an honorary doctorate from the [University of South Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Australia "University of South Australia") in 2015.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peter_Gabriel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Gabriel was born in [Chobham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chobham "Chobham"), Surrey, on 13 February 1950, the son of Edith Irene (née Allen, 1921–2016) and Ralph Parton Gabriel (1912–2012).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201825-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Full_Moon-18) His mother, who came from a musical family, was the daughter of [Colonel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonel_(British_Army) "Colonel (British Army)") Edward Allen, who was the chairman of the [Civil Service Department Store](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_Service_Supply_Association "Civil Service Supply Association") on the [Strand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strand,_London "Strand, London").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201825-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Full_Moon-18) His father, who was the son of Christopher Burton Gabriel (1876–1947), was an electrical-engineer and dairy-farm owner from a family of London timber merchants.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201825-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Full_Moon-18) His great-great-great-uncle, [Sir Thomas Gabriel, 1st Baronet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Thomas_Gabriel,_1st_Baronet "Sir Thomas Gabriel, 1st Baronet"), was [Lord Mayor of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lord_Mayor_of_London "Lord Mayor of London") from 1866 to 1877.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Telegraph_2007-11-24-19)

Gabriel was raised at Deep Pool Farm, a [Victorian manor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_house "Country house"), near Chobham.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201825-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Full_Moon-18) He attended the private primary-school Cable House, [Woking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woking "Woking"), and St. Andrews Preparatory School for Boys, [Horsell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horsell "Horsell"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201825-17) at the latter of which his teachers noticed his singing talent, but he focussed on piano lessons from his mother.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201826-20) He also developed an interest in drumming and, when aged 10 years, bought a [floor tom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floor_tom "Floor tom").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201826-20)

Gabriel later remarked of his early influences, "[Hymns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hymn "Hymn") played quite a large part. They were the closest I came to [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") before I discovered soul music. There are certain hymns that you can scream your lungs out on, and I used to love that. It was great when you used to get the old shivers down the back."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-White_Shadow_pp12-21) He wrote his first song, "Sammy the Slug", at age 12. An aunt gave him money for professional singing-lessons around this time, which he used to buy [the Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles")' debut album _[Please Please Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Please\_Please\_Me "Please Please Me")_ soon after its release.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201826-20) In September 1963, he started at the [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_school_(United_Kingdom) "Public school (United Kingdom)")[Charterhouse School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charterhouse_School "Charterhouse School"), [Godalming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godalming "Godalming").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrame198323-22) There, he was a drummer and vocalist for his first band, the [trad jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trad_jazz "Trad jazz") outfit called the Milords (or M'Lords). This was followed by a holiday band called the Spoken Word,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEaslea201834-23) which recorded an [acetate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acetate_disc "Acetate disc") in 1966.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti202016-24) Gabriel played drums in both these bands, with [Mike Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Rutherford "Mike Rutherford") later commenting, "Pete was—and still is, I think—a frustrated drummer."[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-Mike_on_Mike-25)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peter_Gabriel&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 1965–1975: Early career and Genesis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Peter_Gabriel&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1965–1975: Early career and Genesis")]

In 1965, while still at Charterhouse, Gabriel formed the band [Garden Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garden_Wall_(band) "Garden Wall (band)") with his schoolmates [Tony Banks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Banks_(musician) "Tony Banks (musician)") on piano, Johnny Trapman on trumpet, and [Chris Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Stewart_(author) "Chris Stewart (author)") on drums.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti202016-24) Banks had started at Charterhouse at the same time as Gabriel, and the two were uninterested in school activities but bonded over music and started to write songs. At their final concert before they broke up, Gabriel wore a [kaftan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaftan "Kaftan") and beads and showered the audience with petals he had picked from neighbouring gardens.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrame198323-22) Garden Wall disbanded in 1967; Gabriel and Banks were invited by their Charterhouse schoolmates [Anthony Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Phillips "Anthony Phillips") and [Mike Rutherford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Rutherford "Mike Rutherford"), who were in their own band at the school called [Anon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anon_(band) "Anon (band)") until it split up the previous year, to work on a demo tape of songs together.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti202017-26) Gabriel and Banks contributed "She Is Beautiful", the first song they wrote together. The tape was sent to Charterhouse alumnus, musician [Jonathan King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_King "Jonathan King"), who was immediately enthusiastic largely due to Gabriel's vocals. He signed the group and suggested that their name be Gabriel's Angels, but this was unpopular with the other members, and they soon settled on his other suggestion of [Genesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genesis_(band) "Genesis (band)").

After King suggested they stick to more straightforward pop, Gabriel and Banks wrote "[The Silent Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Silent_Sun "The Silent Sun")" as a pastiche of the [Bee Gees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bee_Gees "Bee Gees"), one of King's favourite bands. It became Genesis' first single, released in 1968,[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowlerDray199217-27) and was included on their debut studio album _[From Genesis to Revelation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From\_Genesis\_to\_Revelation "From Genesis to Revelation")_ (1968). Following the commercial failure of _From Genesis to Revelation_, the band went their separate ways, and Gabriel continued his studies at Charterhouse.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowlerDray199222-28) In September 1969, Gabriel, Banks, Rutherford, and Phillips decided to drop their plans and make Genesis a full-time band. In early 1970, Gabriel played the flute on _[Mona Bone Jakon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona\_Bone\_Jakon "Mona Bone Jakon")_ by [Cat Stevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_Stevens "Cat Stevens"). The second studio album by Genesis, _[Trespass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trespass\_(album) "Trespass (album)")_ (1970), marked Gabriel expanding his musical output with the flute, accordion, tambourine, and bass drum, and incorporating his [soul music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soul_music "Soul music") influences. Gabriel explained that he was driven to play these instruments because he was uncomfortable with doing nothing during instrumental sections.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti202084-29) He would have preferred to play keyboard instruments, but said, "[Banks] was extraordinarily possessive about the keyboards. I'd done a bit of flute at school, I always liked the sound, and a little bit of oboe (I was an even worse oboe player, but it made a couple of good noises now and again). Then the bass drum was something physical, visual, that I could kick hard and occasionally it was in time!"[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti202054-30) The album sold few copies, with Gabriel at one point securing a place to study at the [London School of Film Technique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Film_School "London Film School") because the band "seemed to be dying".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-31)

Genesis soon recruited guitarist [Steve Hackett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Hackett "Steve Hackett") and drummer [Phil Collins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Collins "Phil Collins").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBowlerDray199243-32) Gabriel began growing in confidence as a frontman; during an encore performance of "[The Knife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Knife_(song) "The Knife (song)")" on 19 June 1971, he took a running jump into the audience and expected them to catch him, only for them to instead move out of the way and leave him to land on the floor and break his ankle. He consequently had to perform Genesis' next several shows with a wheelchair and crutches.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti202083-33) Also during the _Trespass_ tour, he started to recite stories to introduce songs as a way to cover the silence while the band tuned their instruments or technical faults were being fixed.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-34) These stories were all improvised on the spot, and evolved as the tour went along.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti202084-29) The opener of their next studio album, _[Nursery Cryme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nursery\_Cryme "Nursery Cryme")_ (1971), "[The Musical Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Musical_Box_(Genesis_song) "The Musical Box (Genesis song)")", was their first song in which Gabriel incorporated a story and characters into the lyrics, as the lyrics to previous story-based Genesis songs such as "White Mountain" and "One-Eyed Hound" were all written by other members of the group.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Gabriel was the primary writer of "Harold the Barrel", another story song on _Nursery Cryme_, with Collins helping him on the lyrics.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Gabriel#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGiammetti2020104-35)

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Peter_Gabriel_The_Moonlight_Knight_%28cropped%29.png/250px-Peter_Gabriel_The_Moonlight_Knight_%28cropped%29.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Peter_Gabriel_The_Moonlight_Knight_(cropped).png)

Gabriel as "[Britannia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britannia "Britannia")" or "[The Moonlit Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_with_the_Moonlit_Knight "Dancing with the Moonlit Knight")" in 1974

The shows featuring _[Foxtrot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foxtrot\_(album) "Foxtrot (album)")_ (1972) marked a key development in Gabriel's stage performance. During a show in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin") in September 1972, he disappeared from the set during the instrumental section of "[The Musical Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Musical_Box_(Genesis_song) "The Musical Box (Genesis song)")" and reappeared in his wife's red dress and a fox's head, mimicking the album's cover.
